Candidates backed by twice-elected former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League-N party have won 24 of the 34 seats decided in the first two phases of voting, said Raja Shakeel, a spokesman for the regional election commission. Turnout exceeded 56% in the regional capital.

Shakee said voting for the remaining 11 seats is scheduled for Aug. 10, but the party is already on course to form the next regional government.

Sponsor Message

It marks the party's return to power in Pakistan-administered Kashmir after a decade.

Shakeel said the elections are being held in three phases because of security concerns and heavy monsoon rains, which have complicated campaigning and made it difficult to hold large outdoor rallies.

According to regional government and election officials said turnout exceeded 50% in many areas, including Muzaffarabad, despite security concerns and calls for a boycott by the outlawed Joint Awami Action Committee, or JAAC, which is notorious for holding violent protests.

Sharif congratulated the winning candidates in a statement.

Pakistan and India each administer part of Kashmir but claim the Himalayan region in its entirety. The nuclear-armed neighbors have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir since gaining independence from Britain in 1947.

The election campaign was overshadowed by weeks of protests led by the JAAC, which in recent weeks has been urging residents not to vote. The regional government recently banned the group, citing security and public-order concerns.

Supporters of the group repeatedly clashed with police ahead of Sunday's vote, but residents said they exercised their right of vote despite fears of violence. Analysts said the election reinforced public confidence in the democratic process, with voters choosing to cast ballots despite weeks of protests, violence and a boycott campaign by the JAAC.

Sponsor Message

The dispute has centered on 12 seats reserved for people displaced from Indian-controlled Kashmir since the end of British colonial rule. The JAAC argues the seats give disproportionate political influence to people living outside Pakistan-administered Kashmir and has demanded they be abolished.

The controversy intensified in June when the region's Supreme Court ruled the seats are protected under the constitution and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The seats were created to ensure representation for people displaced from Indian-controlled Kashmir who settled elsewhere in Pakistan because Pakistan-administered Kashmir lacked the capacity to accommodate them. Many have lived in Pakistan' for decades, while others later moved to Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

Authorities often accuse JAAC supporters of trying to disrupt the election and alleged that members of the Pakistani Taliban had infiltrated the protests. The JAAC has not responded to the allegations.

The group, formed in 2023, demands greater political rights for the people of Kashmir and the government says it had accepted 36 out of the 38 demands, and the issue of reserved seats can only be resolved by the assembly.

World.title: Under China's new 'unity' law, Tibetans fight to preserve language and culture
World.content:
Under China's new 'unity' law, Tibetans fight to preserve language and culture

toggle caption Ng Han Guan/AP

LHASA, Tibet — Kalsang Lhamo traces a series of vertical strokes, slow but firm, practicing Tibetan calligraphy. A 73-year-old retired nurse, she has spoken Tibetan all her life but never learned to write it. Now, in classes at a center for older adults, she immerses herself in the script.

Lhamo also speaks and writes Chinese, which China mandated as its primary language for schools and government agencies in a sweeping new "ethnic unity" law implemented July 1. Under the new regulations, acts deemed to incite division among China's 56 ethnic groups are prohibited, and schools, families and other institutions are expected to foster patriotism, national unity and a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.

Sponsor Message

The law has been widely criticized as a way to further erode the rights of Tibetans and other minorities, and for the authority it gives Beijing to target activities it considers separatist, even outside China. The Chinese government has dismissed foreign criticism as "ideological bias."

In Tibet — a remote Himalayan region officially designated autonomous but tightly controlled by Beijing — the stakes are particularly high. This year, China is marking the 75th anniversary of what it calls the "peaceful liberation" of Xizang — the Chinese name for Tibet — an event many Tibetans in exile and other critics regard as an invasion.

Some Tibetan activists say the new law represents more forced cultural assimilation and extended control over ethnic minorities. Rights groups say language policies have already been implemented in other minority regions, including expanded Mandarin education for Uyghurs in Xinjiang and the replacement of some Mongolian-language instruction with Mandarin in Inner Mongolia.

"Minority communities that seek to maintain their culture will be pushed toward a double life of public conformity and private reservations," wrote James Leibold from La Trobe University and Tenzin Dorjee from the advocacy group Tibet Action Institute in Foreign Affairs magazine.

The Associated Press last month joined a government-organized trip to Tibet, including stops in the regional capital, Lhasa, and the city of Shannan, where authorities arranged visits to palaces, Buddhist temples, tourist sites, local businesses and the eldercare center where Lhamo studies. Government officials accompanied the foreign journalists throughout the visit, and AP journalists were not free to move around or conduct reporting independently. The AP retained full editorial control of its content.

Sponsor Message

Reminders that Tibet is part of China are everywhere, from Chinese airport welcome messages and billboards promoting ethnic unity to Chinese national flags and President Xi Jinping portraits in public squares and buildings.

Some Tibetans, like Lhamo, have found ways to embrace their language and identity, even as critics say the new law pushes China's majority Han culture. In Tibet, that can mean studying the Tibetan script, speaking it at home and with family members, preserving traditional weaving and attending Buddhist rituals.

toggle caption Ng Han Guan/AP

At these religious sites in Tibet, no signs or references to the Dalai Lama

At the Jokhang Temple, one of Tibet's holiest religious sites, Tibetans and Han Chinese visited. Some rested outside. Most people in Tibet practice Tibetan Buddhism.

"As a Tibetan, I think it's important to preserve our language and our culture," said Qongqiu Quco, a 19-year-old student who came with her aunts, some of them Buddhist nuns.

"Everyone in our ethnic group hopes that our culture can be passed down to future generations," said Quco, an aspiring teacher who speaks Tibetan much of the time. But at school, she noted, students speak different Tibetan dialects, so they use Mandarin.

For Tibetan Buddhists, the Dalai Lama is their spiritual leader. But at Jokhang Temple, there are no signs or references to the current Dalai Lama, who has lived in exile since fleeing to India after a failed 1959 uprising against Chinese rule.

The succession of the 14th Dalai Lama, who established a government-in-exile unrecognized by Beijing, has become one of the most contentious issues surrounding Tibet. The Dalai Lama has said his successor could be born outside China and that only his office has the authority to recognize his reincarnation.

Beijing says the selection must comply with Chinese law and receive government approval. China has long accused the Dalai Lama of promoting separatism.

Sponsor Message

The Potala Palace, one of Tibet's most revered sites and once the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, also had no public reference to the current leader. Thousands visit daily — tourists from across China and local Buddhist believers who pray and leave offerings, including money.

Today, the Chinese national flag flies there.

toggle caption Ng Han Guan/AP

China's unity law 'codifies' a policy that's already playing out, an expert says

Benno Weiner, a professor and historian on modern China and Tibet at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, said many effects of the policy shift have already been visible for years — particularly stripped-away education and language rights.

"I don't think the law itself changes things," he said. "I think it sort of codifies and sort of summarizes a trend that's been going on."

Beijing says the policies improve educational opportunities and ensure equal access for ethnic minorities.

The same week as AP's government-organized trip, China's No. 4-ranked Communist Party leader, Wang Huning, toured Tibet, where he said the priority in governing the region was maintaining stability. He called for the implementation of the unity law and urged authorities to "guide Tibetan Buddhism to adapt to socialist society," according to a report by state news agency Xinhua.

On its trip, AP visited a traditional Tibetan medicine facility; artisan workshops and cultural centers with traditional crafts, including ceramic making and textile weaving; and a Tibetan opera performance, where workers and performers spoke about the importance of preserving local traditions.

Weiner noted that the Chinese government's approach to cultural preservation often emphasizes elements seen as less politically sensitive and suitable for tourism.

"The parts of culture that they want to protect and maybe even enhance are the sort of anodyne or nondangerous clothing, certain celebrations that are not religious in many cases," he said. "Things that maybe not that coincidentally also attract tourists."

Sponsor Message

At the Tibet Museum, an exhibit highlights Tibet's historical links with Chinese dynasties over centuries, a narrative Beijing uses to argue that Tibet has long been part of China. Many Tibetans in exile dispute that, arguing that Tibet was independent for much of its history.

Laba Ciren, the Communist Party's official in charge of the museum, spoke to journalists about the new law. "It only brings benefits and does not have any negative effects," he said.

Billboards carry the law's message: Promote integration

Access to Tibet is tightly restricted for foreigners. But for those who do arrive, a first observation — after the thinner air, with Lhasa Gonggar International Airport at 3,600 meters (11,800 feet) elevation — might be the official welcome messages.

Some signs are written in Chinese and Tibetan. But outside the terminal, a large sign, in Chinese, says simply: "Xizang welcomes you."

From highways to city streets in Lhasa and Shannan, billboards promoting ethnic unity are a constant presence. In part, one reads, in Mandarin and then Tibetan: "Forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation."

In Lhasa, Lhamo retired 22 years ago. With her children grown, she tries to make it to classes at the center every day — writing, grammar, poetry — in part because she wasn't able to attend school as a child.

"Our mother tongue is the Tibetan language," she said proudly.

World.title: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic primary for Senate
World.content:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic primary for Senate

toggle caption Nic Antaya/AP

Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, according to a race call by The Associated Press. The result marks a win for the progressive wing of the party, with El-Sayed defeating Rep. Haley Stevens, who had the backing of party centrists.

Vote counting went through the night and into the morning before the race was decided. Now El-Sayed will face former Rep. Mike Rogers this fall for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The match up is seen as a must-win for Democrats hoping to retake the chamber from Republican control.

Sponsor Message

"We know that to defeat Trumpism we have to defeat Trump's handpicked candidate," El-Sayed told NPR's Morning Edition shortly before the race was called.

Loading...

El-Sayed is an epidemiologist and a former health director for Detroit and later the surrounding county. He ran for governor in 2018 but came in second to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, in the primary.

His platform includes embracing Medicare for all and cutting the influence of corporate money in politics. During his campaign he highlighted and criticized the money being spent against him by an organization aligned with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC.

He attracted the biggest stars on the political left, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who traveled to Michigan to campaign with him.

El-Sayed does not identify as a socialist and calls himself a capitalist. While he is not endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, whose candidates have won races this primary season, he holds some similar positions. He supports abolishing ICE, for example.

He was up against Stevens, a four-term congresswoman who flipped a suburban House seat in 2018 and served on the team President Obama tasked with rescuing the auto industry during the 2008-2009 recession. She pledged to fight Trump on his tariffs and rising costs because of the war with Iran and focused on her support for Michigan manufacturing.

Sponsor Message

Stevens' supporters had argued that she would have had a better chance of winning in a purple state in November's general election.

El-Sayed had been leading the polls in the primary contest while Stevens had the money advantage with groups that supported her outspending El-Sayed's on the airwaves by several times, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm.

Voters had to decide between two millennial Democrats vying to beat Rogers.

The Senate primary became a test of how candidates further left on the political spectrum will fare outside liberal cities where they have won elections earlier this year.

Michigan is a swing state. After Joe Biden won Michigan in 2020, Donald Trump carried the state in 2024, even as Democrat Elissa Slotkin narrowly won an open Senate seat that had been held by Democrats.

NPR's Sam Gringlas contributed to this story.

World.title: U.S. missile stockpiles dwindle. And, FDA weighs approval of flu shots with mRNA tech
World.content:
U.S. missile stockpiles dwindle. And, FDA weighs approval of flu shots with mRNA tech

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The U.S. Army has used most of its long-range attack missiles in the war with Iran, NPR has confirmed. A U.S. official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said that precision missiles like PrSMs and ATCAMs are nearly depleted. These offensive weapons can strike from hundreds of miles away, providing crucial protection for U.S. servicemembers by reducing the need for American pilots to approach enemy targets closely.

U.S. Navy/Getty Images

🎧 Despite these shortages , senior military officials say the U.S. currently has enough offensive weapons to meet its immediate needs, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. But these precision missiles take years to replenish, which means depleted stockpiles could leave the U.S. vulnerable in future conflicts. The U.S. stockpile of Patriot interceptors, which are the U.S.' main tool to shoot down drones and missiles in the Middle East, has shrunk by two-thirds since the start of this war, according to a Center for Strategic and International Studies report. Patriots also take a significant amount of time to replenish, and they cost around $4 million each.

, senior military officials say the U.S. currently has enough offensive weapons to meet its immediate needs, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. But these precision missiles take years to replenish, which means depleted stockpiles could leave the U.S. vulnerable in future conflicts. The U.S. stockpile of Patriot interceptors, which are the U.S.' main tool to shoot down drones and missiles in the Middle East, has shrunk by two-thirds since the start of this war, according to a Center for Strategic and International Studies report. Patriots also take a significant amount of time to replenish, and they cost around $4 million each. ➡️ The shrinking stockpile of Patriot missiles also leaves U.S. allies vulnerable. Ukraine currently faces an urgent need for a fresh supply to defend itself against Russia.

Sponsor Message

Michigan's closely watched Democratic Senate primary is too close to call. Progressive Abdul El-Sayed currently has a narrow lead over moderate Congresswoman Haley Stevens. The winner will compete for a vital Senate seat against Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in a swing state crucial to Democrats' efforts to regain control of the chamber. Here's what you need to know about all of yesterday's primary races in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington.



🎧 The mood among Democratic voters has shifted since the 2018 midterm during President Trump's first term, according to NPR's Tamara Keith. At that time, moderate Democrats were seen as the solution. This time, Democratic primary voters blame their own party for the president's win, Keith says. She adds that the party has significant repair work to do, regardless of who wins in Michigan. The bitter primary has left some voters saying they're unwilling to support the opposing candidate in November.

The Food and Drug Administration is deciding whether to approve the first flu vaccine that uses mRNA technology. Moderna's mFlusiva vaccine would operate similarly to its COVID-19 vaccine by stimulating the immune system to produce antibodies that can fight off viruses. Its approval has been met with skepticism due to scrutiny over mRNA technology stemming from anger over COVID-19 vaccine mandates during the pandemic and misinformation about the shot's safety.



Sponsor Message

🎧 A trial of over 40,000 participants showed that Moderna's mFlusiva is safe and offers stronger protection than traditional flu shots for adults 50 and older, NPR's Rob Stein says. The vaccine earned a unanimous recommendation for approval from independent FDA advisers in June. Beyond providing stronger protection, the mRNA vaccine can be reformulated and produced more quickly than traditional options, allowing experts to adapt more quickly to new flu strains or pandemics.

Central Appalachian veteran underground coal miners are experiencing an incurable and fatal lung disease at the highest rates recorded in nearly 50 years, according to the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Miners who have worked underground for at least 25 years in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia suffer the worst rates of coal workers' pneumoconiosis, also known as black lung disease. The disease's prevalence hit a low point in 1999, after Congress imposed strict limits on exposure to the coal mine dust that causes black lung. But the decline in cases has been reversed, and experts blame toxic silica dust that is now more common in mines.

Deep dive

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) will undergo a restructuring of its funding model in October. But even before the changes take effect, more than 4 million Americans — many of whom are children — have lost access to its critical food aid. SNAP started to see a rapid decline in participation during the same month that the Trump administration's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included major changes to the program, became law. Program eligibility has been tightened, and once the funding model shift happens, states will face increased costs that could lead them to scale back or withdraw from the program. According to Starsky Wilson from the Children's Defense Fund, such cuts could leave food banks and government programs unable to fill the gap. Here's how the program works, where things stand and what's changed.



Sponsor Message

🛒 To access food benefits, adults must work or volunteer 80 hours each month. This now applies to veterans, homeless individuals, young adults aging out of foster care, parents of 14- to 17-year-olds and those aged 55 to 64.

🛒 As of April, 37 million Americans used food stamps each month, marking an 11% decline since last July.

🛒 Starting in October, states will be responsible for covering 75% of operational expenses, while the federal government will contribute only 25%.

Behind the story

by Cory Turner , NPR Ed correspondent

toggle caption Kieran Kesner for NPR

So much of the public discussion around the use of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools seems to focus on one thing: cheating. How and how often are teens using chatbots to do their thinking for them, write their papers or help them race through their homework?

These fears may be well-founded — a generation mistaking what researchers call cognitive offloading for real learning would be calamitous — but, as a reporter, I've been eager for a chance to center teen voices in this discussion. I wanted to hear them voice their fears, but also their solutions.

That's why I gave an enthusiastic "yes" when a handful of groups approached me to ask if I would be interested in covering a convening of 100 students, two from every state, in a kind of mock Senate debate. These student senators had a goal of doing what the nation's actual lawmakers have so far failed to do: draft a national policy for the use of AI in K-12 schools.

The students met over a frantic, late-July weekend in Boston in an exact, scale replica of the U.S. Senate chamber. I got full access to the teens as they wrote, debated, made new friends and gave impassioned floor speeches about the risks and rewards of AI.

One particular moment that stood out to me had nothing to do with cheating. The teens were debating what to do if a student in crisis tries to use a school chatbot for emotional support.

Sponsor Message

A high-schooler from Iowa, Dylan Dornack, argued that it was important the AI not be allowed to respond and that, instead, a small group of trusted school officials be alerted.

"This could be life-saving," Dornack said, "This is just one of those things that has to be taken to trusted adults."

After Dornack made his case to the full Senate, the amendment passed overwhelmingly.

I hope you'll read more about what I saw and what students could agree on when it comes to AI at school.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images

In SpaceX's first quarterly report since going public, the company beat expectations, reporting nearly double the previous year's revenue and narrowing losses, but posted no profit. Maryland has opened the country's largest center for human composting. This process, which takes about a month, transforms human remains into nutrient-rich soil using bacteria, fungi, and mulch. (via WYPR) When Annabelle Gurwitch was undergoing cancer treatment in 2020, she couldn't imagine what her future would look like. But her unsung hero gave her an unexpectedly raunchy piece of advice right before a date, encouraging her to start re-engaging with life.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Russian missile and drone barrage in Ukrainian capital region kills 17
World.content:
Russian missile and drone barrage in Ukrainian capital region kills 17

toggle caption Dan Bashakov/AP

KYIV, Ukraine — Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region killed 17 people and wounded 44 others overnight into Wednesday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack was the latest in a series of large-scale Russian ballistic missile strikes that have become near-routine this summer. The intensified barrages are exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of interceptor missiles for the U.S.-made Patriot systems, the sole air defense system in its arsenal able to shoot down ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has pleaded with other countries to send more of the ammunition made scarcer by the Iran war.

"Ballistic interceptors are what could have saved the lives of those killed today," Zelenskyy said on social media. "It is very important for our partners to understand that delays in supplying them, or a reluctance to hand over anti-ballistic systems, lead directly to such horrific casualties and destruction."

Sponsor Message

Ukraine hits back with long-range drones

With U.S.-led peace efforts apparently stalled, Ukraine has stepped up its deep strikes on key Russian targets such as oil refineries in an effort to compel Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate. Zelenskyy has accepted an unconditional ceasefire demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump but Putin has refused.

In its latest attack on logistics facilities of Wildberries, Russia's biggest online retailer, Ukrainian drones hit a warehouse in the Tula region south of Moscow, the company and the region's governor said Wednesday.

It was the 14th Wildberries warehouse to catch fire in less than three weeks, according to a Ukrainian tally. Ukraine says the company provides goods that can be used by the military. Kyiv is also keen to unsettle the Russian public with high-profile attacks.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces downed 475 Ukrainian drones overnight over 16 Russian regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

Russia says it struck war-related targets in the Kyiv region

Russia fired 24 ballistic missiles, four other missiles identified as either hypersonic Zircons or supersonic Oniks, and 115 drones, many of them jet-powered, in the attack, Ukrainian authorities said.

Sponsor Message

The strikes mainly targeted warehouses belonging to civilian businesses, Zelenskyy said, as well as infrastructure and a railway station — sites that he said have "no connection to the war," including a brewing company, building materials warehouses and civilian logistics facilities.

But the Russian Defense Ministry said it struck transport, logistics and distribution centers involved in military activity. It listed four targets in Kyiv, claiming they ran war-related operations.

It was not immediately possible to reconcile the different accounts.

Ukraine's largest private postal operator, Nova Poshta, said a Russian cluster munition destroyed one of its sorting centers in Kyiv.

The Russian Defense Ministry said the center was "storing and distributing dual-use goods, including those used in the production of long- and medium-range uncrewed aerial vehicles, as well as robotic systems and electronic warfare systems." It claimed that two other logistics centers in the Kyiv region stored drones or components for drones.

Separately, the ministry said its forces hit three bulk carriers on the Black Sea south of Odesa that it claimed were transporting weapons and military equipment for the Ukrainian armed forces. Ukrainian officials didn't comment on that claim.

Truck drivers make a narrow escape

Ivan Braga, a 46-year-old truck driver from Moldova who was in Kyiv during the attack, said he and a colleague ran from their vehicle when it was struck by shrapnel in a blast wave.

"We didn't even have time to grab our documents or anything else," Braga told The Associated Press. "I couldn't believe it. I'd already been in Kyiv and had heard explosions before, but nothing like today."

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology development, said the war of attrition has entered a new phase. "The enemy is attacking everything indiscriminately — retail warehouses, food storage facilities, logistics hubs, enterprises, building materials warehouses," he said on Facebook.

Sponsor Message

One of the companies that came under heavy fire was Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest retail and construction chains. It said in a statement on Facebook that "in minutes, Russian missiles destroyed what the company had built over decades." One employee was killed and three others were wounded.

According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the Epicenter logistics center handled order processing, sorting, storing, and delivery of dual-use goods and components for drone production.

World.title: Progressives see biggest win yet in Michigan, while Trump flexes power over GOP
World.content:
Progressives see biggest win yet in Michigan, while Trump flexes power over GOP

toggle caption Bill Pugliano/Getty Images

Everyone got a little bit of what they wanted in Tuesday's primary elections. It was a good night for the Democratic establishment, the progressives and Republican candidates endorsed by President Trump.

Some of the primary races for House and Senate in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington are critical to which party will hold power in the next Congress.

The results following the primary elections indicate a clear split between the establishment and progressive arms of the Democratic Party, while Trump continues to flex his power with Republicans. But voters also pushed back against Republican Party priorities in a pair of ballot initiatives in red states.

Progressive power tested

It was a huge primary win for the progressive side of the Democratic Party. Voters in Michigan picked progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed as the Democratic nominee for Senate. He beat Rep. Haley Stevens, who was backed by the establishment wing of the party and has taken a more moderate approach to the race.

Sponsor Message

The race was the biggest test for progressives to see if their populist agenda, such as Medicare for All, would bode well in a true swing state. If Democrats want to take control of the U.S. Senate in November, winning the seat is crucial to accomplishing that goal.

But the outcome of the Democratic primary makes it clear there is a stark divide among Democratic primary voters and the qualities they want to see from a sitting senator. Whoever wins the primary will face a tough challenge from the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Progressives also picked up a win in Michigan's one true toss-up district. Progressive William Lawrence beat two other Democrats for the nomination. Lawrence is set to challenge first-term incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett in November. In Michigan's 13th Congressional District, Donavan McKinney unseated Rep. Shri Thanedar.

Establishment Democrats got the candidates they wanted in a few key races. In Missouri's 1st Congressional District, Rep. Wesley Bell won a rematch against former Rep. Cori Bush. Bell was backed by the national party, while Bush clenched endorsements from democratic socialists and high-profile progressives, such as Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Related: Bell defeats Bush in contentious 1st Congressional District Democratic primary rematch

Sponsor Message

Bell will face Republican nominee Paul Berry in November, though Cook Political Report rates the district as solidly Democratic.

In Virginia, Democratic voters picked establishment-backed candidates for two House seats. The two seats, Virginia's 1st and 2nd congressional districts, are ones Democrats hope to flip in November to inch toward the party's goal of taking control of the chamber.

toggle caption Bill Pugliano/Getty Images

Money in politics a bit of a mixed bag

One of the rallying cries of the progressive left has been to "get money out of politics." As the spending in Michigan's Senate race ballooned, El-Sayed specifically criticized a pro-Israel political action committee, AIPAC, saying the organization had too much influence in politics. AIPAC and its aligned groups spent millions of dollars backing Stevens in the Democratic primary — money that it's not clear paid off.

According to Open Secrets, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that tracks congressional candidate fundraising and spending, by mid-July, outside groups had spent $52 million in Michigan. That's the most expensive use of outside spending apart from Texas' contentious and protracted Senate race.

In the race in St. Louis, Rep. Bell's commitment to fund humanitarian and military aid to Israel saw AIPAC back his candidacy in a safe blue seat, to prevent another candidate, who might be critical of Israel, from taking that seat.

Trump's influence remains strong with Republicans

Trump-backed candidates in Washington state, Kansas and Michigan won their party's nomination.

In Washington's 4th Congressional District, Trump endorsed Yakima County Commissioner Amanda McKinney. She beat 10 other candidates for the top spot. The wide-open seat is to replace outgoing Republican Congressman Dan Newhouse — one of the only Republicans still in office who voted to impeach Trump in 2021.

toggle caption Scott Olson/Getty Images

McKinney received Trump's endorsement, but it didn't come with any certainty. A Trump-endorsed candidate has never won a general election in the conservative, rural district, although there is a possibility that could change since Newhouse is not on the ballot. McKinney will face Democrat John Duresky in November.

Sponsor Message

Trump-backed candidates also won the Republican nomination for governor in Michigan and Kansas. Democrats currently hold the office in both states, but Republicans are hoping to take the mansion back since the sitting governors are term-limited.

In Michigan, Republican Rep. John James won the nomination. He'll face off against Michigan's Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson. In Kansas, Republican state Sen. Ty Masterson clinched the nomination. Masterson faces a challenge from Cindy Holscher, another state senator.

While Trump won both states in 2024, Michigan and Kansas have different electorates. Michigan is a swing state, and Democrats have hung on to the office since 2018. Kansas, on the other hand, is solidly red. Even though there has been a Democratic governor running the state for the last two election cycles, it's unclear if that can happen again.

The three races show Trump's grip on the Republican base, despite record-low approval ratings over the state of the economy and the U.S. involvement in the Iran war.

Bad night for Republican-backed ballot initiatives

It was a tough loss for two Republican-led ballot initiatives in Missouri and Kansas.

No changes to the state Supreme Court bench are happening in Kansas' future. Voters there rejected a Republican-backed proposal for state Supreme Court justices to be elected instead of appointed.

Currently, judges for the state's highest court are appointed by the governor based on choices presented by a nominating committee. Most of the court has been appointed by the current and previous governors, both Democrats elected in the mostly Republican state. The court has upheld abortion rights, among other stands objected to by Republican leaders.

Voters in Missouri voted against a proposal by the Republican-led legislature to make it harder for the public to pass future amendments to the state constitution.

After an amendment passed in recent years to end the legislature's strict ban on abortion and another that expanded Medicaid, the legislature proposed a question on Tuesday's ballot that would have raised the bar.

Currently, approval just requires a majority vote statewide. The defeated amendment would have required a majority vote in each of the state's eight congressional districts. None of the recent amendments would have passed if that were the threshold.

World.title: B.C. wildfire conditions 'explosive and extremely dangerous' as crews brace for more heat, dry lightning
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The latest on the wildfires:

The Pear Lake wildfire is the largest burning in B.C. right now, at roughly 1,247 square kilometres. The Thompson-Nicola Regional District says about 120 properties , not including the Village of Clinton, have suffered structural loss.

, not including the Village of Clinton, have suffered structural loss. The chief of the Okanagan Indian Band estimates at least 200 homes have been destroyed by the Bradley Creek wildfire, west of Vernon. It's grown to roughly 28.5 square kilometers.

by the Bradley Creek wildfire, west of Vernon. It's grown to The Regional District of Northern Okanagan expanded an evacuation order on Tuesday, due to the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires, to include several dozen more properties.

on Tuesday, due to the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires, to include several dozen more properties. Across B.C., about 8,000 people are under evacuation order and 7,100 are under evacuation alert.

Wildfire officials say conditions are "explosive and extremely dangerous," with a forecast of hot temperatures and potential lightning ahead.

Hotter weather returns

The period of cooler, more humid weather that provided some relief for crews battling the Pear Lake wildfire has come to an end, according to the B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS).

It says hotter, drier conditions have returned and are expected to increase fire activity in the coming days.

In the southern Interior, temperatures are expected to hit the mid-30s this week, with the possibility of dry lightning.

Of the 116 wildfires burning across B.C., 87 are believed to have been caused by lightning. Eight new fires started in the last 24 hours.

Sunset in Kelowna, B.C., on Tuesday, Aug. 4, as wildfires burn nearby. (Jay Bertagnolli/CBC)

The BCWS said Wednesday that winds are forecast to remain "light" in most areas.

That's a welcome reprieve from last weekend when 80 km/h winds and 115 km/h gusts quickly spread the Bradley Creek fire near Vernon.

"We are seeing fuel conditions that we have never seen before. We are seeing fire behaviour and fire growth that we have never experienced in B.C. up until this point," said BCWS director of wildfire operations Cliff Chapman Tuesday.

"It is an explosive and extremely dangerous situation."

A helicopter conducting night operations prepares to drop water on the Quilpituk Creek wildfire on Monday, Aug. 3. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Homes destroyed

Officials say hundreds of properties have been damaged or destroyed in multiple parts of the province.

The Thompson-Nicola Regional District says about 120 properties have experienced structure loss from the Pear Lake wildfire, excluding the Village of Clinton.

The hardest-hit places include Big Bar Lake, south of Clinton near Highway 97, an area west of Clinton around Kelly Lake Road and the Chasm area north of the village.

District spokesperson Clinton Davies said the number will likely increase as crews safely reach more affected areas.

West of Vernon, Okanagan Indian Band Chief Dan Wilson estimates the Bradley Creek wildfire has destroyed at least 200 homes, though the figure is preliminary.

He said the fire has been “one of the most devastating events in our history," and many people in the community have lost everything they own.

Properties on Okanagan Indian Band land that were destroyed by the Bradley Creek wildfire are seen on Tuesday, Aug. 4. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

B.C. Hydro says an early investigation has found "significant damage" to its infrastructure in some areas. Public affairs coordinator Dave Cooper said at least 150 power poles in the Bradley Creek fire area will need to be replaced.

Crews have not yet been able to finish their assessment of the area around the Quilpituk Creek fire, but Cooper said he expects there will be more poles there that need to be repaired and replaced.

He said crews will begin work once it's safe to do so.

Evacuation orders

About 8,000 people across B.C. are under evacuation order, while another 7,100 are under evacuation alert and have been told to be ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

Anyone placed under an evacuation order should leave the area immediately.

Many of those impacted are being threatened by the Quilpituk Creek and Bradley Creek wildfires, both burning along Okanagan Lake.

The Central Okanagan Emergency Operations Centre says 2,223 properties remain under evacuation order due to the Quilpituk Creek fire, while another 425 properties are under evacuation alert.

Numerous properties on Okanagan Indian Band land, seen here on Tuesday, Aug. 4, have been destroyed by wildfire. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

The Regional District of Northern Okanagan expanded an evacuation order on Tuesday, as a result of both fires, to include several dozen more properties.

Evacuation orders also cover the Okanagan Indian Band.

The Spallumcheen evacuation order and alert areas related to the Bradley Creek fire were shrunken on Tuesday.

Those in need of emergency support services are being directed to the Westbank Lions Community Centre in West Kelowna and Kal Tire Place in Vernon.

A map showing the expanded evacuation order for the Bradley Creek and Quilpituk Creek wildfires as of Aug. 4. (Regional District of North Okanagan)

Evacuation orders remain in effect for the French Bar Creek fire in the Thompson-Nicola Regional District, the Pear Lake fire near Clinton and the Brunswick fire complex near Boston Bar, which is now more than 484.17 square kilometres in size.

An evacuation order issued by the Lytton First Nation due to the Riley Creek wildfire was downgraded to an alert earlier this week.

In the East Kootenay, an evacuation order was partially downgraded to an alert on Sunday after crews made progress on the Wait Creek wildfire.

Road closures

According to DriveSafeBC, several major routes remain closed because of wildfire activity.

Highway 1 is closed between Toll Road and Jackass Summit, north of Hells Gate, because of the Brunswick wildfire complex. Drivers are being directed to use highways 3 or 5.

Further north, just past Cache Creek, Highway 97 is closed between Loon Lake Road and 76 Mile Frontage Road. Traffic is being detoured using highways 5 and 8, through Merritt.

Westside Road along Okanagan Lake is closed between Shelter Cove and Highway 97 north, cutting off a key route. The road is open as far as Shelter Cove, with Highway 97 serving as the alternate route.

Toward the U.S. border, Silver Skagit Road is closed south of Flood Hope Road to the Canada-U.S. border because of the Hozomeen Mountain wildfire. Silver Lake remains open, but Ross Lake Campground and Skagit Valley Provincial Park are closed.

Do you have a story to share?

If you've been affected by the B.C. wildfires and want to share your story, email cbcnewsvancouver@cbc.ca.

World.title: 'Everyone's in a super great mood': Dozens line up to cross Gordie Howe bridge for 1st time on bike, by foot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some cyclists and pedestrians said they were “excited” and “overwhelmed” as they crossed the Gordie Howe International Bridge for the first time, using the new multi-use path Wednesday morning.

The path opened at 8 a.m. ET, allowing people to walk or cycle across the bridge linking Windsor, Ont., and Detroit.

“This is a historic moment,” said cyclist Collin Vassell, who crossed from the Canadian side with his wife, Kim.

“Who's going to be able to say that they … rode their bike across the bridge on the ... first day that it was open? Like, seriously.… I was actually overwhelmed with some emotions doing this experience with my wife.”

Cyclists and pedestrians had been unable to cross a bridge between Windsor and Detroit since they were barred from doing so on the Ambassador Bridge decades ago.

On Wednesday morning, people snapped photographs in front of the Canadian and American flags on the path, and vehicles honked their horns as they passed.

'Everyone's in a super great mood'

Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) mascot Buddy the Bear also made an appearance.

Kevin Hinman, who crossed from Detroit with his wife Sophie, said the bridge was less crowded than he expected, so the journey was pleasant.

“Everyone's in a super great mood — got a lot of 'Good mornings' and 'Hellos.'”

Mondrell Pickens, who crossed with 13 other family members, some pushing strollers, said they wanted to make a memory together that they could pass down to their children.

Collin Vassall said he was overcome with emotion as he crossed the Gordie Howe International Bridge by bicycle on Aug. 5, 2026. (Peter Duck/CBC)

“We all wanted to do it together,” he said.

“Something to remember for the rest of our lives, that we all … walked on this bridge when it first was built in Canada.”

Around 100 people were lined up at the Canadian entrance to the path as the gate opened; they were separated from the roadway by yellow tape stretched between orange stanchions.

Among them was Kevin Keeper, dressed in a T-shirt with Canadian and American flags on it. He was hoping to become the first American to cross from the Canadian side.

“I’m just overcome with emotion,” Keeper told CBC.

“It's just so exciting to be here as part of the very first morning and on a sunny day here in beautiful Windsor.”

400 cyclists preparing to cycle from Detroit

The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA) set up porta-potties outside the entrance to the Canadian side of the path for the day.

It also had a covered booth with balloons on hand and bridge merchandise for sale.

On the Detroit side of the river, 400 members of the Gordie Howe International Bike Club were preparing to cross the bridge at 10:15 a.m., organizer Amanda Ray told CBC’s Windsor Morning.

The group hopes to make additional crossings at 1:30 and 6 p.m.

The CBC's Emma Loop crosses the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot | Duration 2:54 The CBC's Emma Loop walks across the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot as the bridge's multi-use path opens on Aug. 5, 2026.

Ray said the goal of the group is to create friendships and connections across the bridge.

“I feel like we have more in common with the Canadians and people that live in Windsor than we do necessarily with people that live in Nebraska."

The WDBA is asking people to be patient as they wait their turn to cross the bridge.

“With the anticipated high number of path users, expect line-ups entering the path and line-ups at border processing,” it wrote on its website.

“WDBA is limiting the number of people that can be on the path at any one time over the initial opening days to support smooth operations.”

The bridge authority estimates it will take people approximately 45 minutes to make the three-kilometre trek on foot from one border inspection booth to the other.

WATCH | Dozens line up to cross Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike: Dozens line up to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike | Duration 4:01 Dozens lined up to cross the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot or by bike Wednesday morning as the bridge's multi-use path opened to the public.

It estimates the same trip will take around 20 minutes by bike.

There is a posted speed limit on the path of 20 km/h.

Both the bridge authority and the CBSA are reminding people to bring their travel documents onto the bridge even if they aren’t planning to cross into the United States.

Path users who return to the Canadian side of the bridge will have to report to the CBSA before exiting, the agency said, and people without proper documentation could be held up while officials try to verify their identity and status.

The bridge authority is also reminding people there is no on-site parking at either port of entry. It's advising people to park at the Malden Park trailhead in Windsor or the Clark Park trailhead in Detroit.

World.title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in major victory for party's progressive wing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Abdul El-Sayed, an insurgent former public health official who harnessed Democratic frustration with the party establishment, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's U.S. Senate primary, setting up a crucial test for progressives in a key battleground state.

El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in a November midterm race that will help determine control of the Senate. His first challenge will be unifying Democratic factions after a bitter primary that offered divergent visions for a party desperate for a path back to power.

Stevens, who pledged her support for El-Sayed after conceding defeat, was backed by the Democratic establishment, including outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, whose retirement spurred a scramble to fill his seat. El-Sayed promised a more aggressive approach for confronting entrenched corporate interests and President Donald Trump, and declared his victory was nothing short of a political earthquake despite only scraping by Stevens.

"In the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world," he said.

Curtis Hertel, the chair of Michigan Democratic Party, urged unity ahead of November.

"We have got to work together to take this country back," Hertel said.

"I can tell you what we need is a fighter," he added. "Abdul El-Sayed has been a fighter for the people over and over again."

WATCH | El-Sayed speaks after victory: Abdul El-Sayed on building a 'people's democracy' after Michigan Democratic Senate primary win | Duration 0:44 Hear some of U.S. Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's remarks after winning Michigan's closely-watched Democratic primary.

The Associated Press declared El-Sayed the winner after confirming — after Wednesday morning updates from Wayne and Oakland counties, two of the state's largest, in the Detroit area in southeastern Michigan — that there were simply not enough votes left to count that would allow Stevens to catch up and overtake him as the leader.

His victory was ultimately so narrow that it wasn't assured until almost all ballots cast statewide were counted. At the time AP declared him the winner, El-Sayed led Stevens by 14,893 votes — a margin of just under one percentage point — out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted.

Progressives gaining strength

El-Sayed's win, however slim, represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party. In 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to Gretchen Whitmer, now the governor, by 21 percentage points.

The former health official campaigned on "Medicare for All," halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.

El-Sayed, left, and Rep. Haley Stevens appear on television during a debate at WoodTV studios on July 7 in Grand Rapids, Mich. (Kristen Norman/The Associated Press)

Stevens — a four-term congresswoman and more moderate candidate — was backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and tens of millions in outside spending, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee's (AIPAC) largest outlay ever in a single race.

Her campaign focused on manufacturing and the economy. She stressed her past victories in tough races, saying she would be best positioned to beat Rogers.

The race for the Senate in November will help decide which party controls the chamber in the last two years of President Donald Trump's term. Those stakes added heat to the primary, with moderates arguing that El-Sayed would have a harder time than Stevens against a Republican in the general election.

Stevens won election to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama's auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. Her campaign and allied groups have repeatedly highlighted that experience.

Clear differences

El-Sayed cast himself as the anti-establishment candidate and argued that Democrats need to reject corporate influence and embrace a more progressive agenda.

While El-Sayed has said he is not a democratic socialist, he found support from some who do. That included Melat Kiros, who recently beat a longtime incumbent in a Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat, and Hasan Piker, a progressive and controversial influencer online.

The candidates' differences were clear to some voters.

LISTEN | What is AIPAC?: Front Burner 35:13 The backlash against AIPAC

Kenneth Woodside, 87, of West Bloomfield, said he voted for El-Sayed over Stevens because "the nation is ready for someone who wants to take some more action rather than on the road we are now, which is on the road to an oligarchy and authoritarianism."

Nessa Fuller, 51, of Birmingham, said she voted for Stevens because she will "fight to get the right things done, and she'll work with other people, which is really important to me."

National groups poured unprecedented sums into the race, making it one of the country's biggest tests of outside spending.

Groups backing Stevens spent more than $50 million US, led by more than $30 million US from AIPAC and its affiliates.

The spending thrust U.S. policy on Israel into the centre of the race even though the ads never mentioned it. While El-Sayed called for ending military aid to Israel, Stevens maintained strong support for the relationship.

Israel became a contentious issue within the Democratic Party amid a war in Gaza that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in its retaliatory offensive after about 1,200 people were killed and 251 hostages were taken in attacks by the militant group Hamas in October 2023.

World.title: This kitten was too tiny for a wheelchair. So his foster mom made one with Hot Wheels and duct tape
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with veterinary assistant Mallory Smith: As It Happens 5:25 Kitten too small for animal wheelchair gets one made of Hot Wheels and duct tape

When Gelato the kitten arrived at a Cincinnati animal shelter last month, injured and unable to use his back legs, he was too tiny for an animal wheelchair.

The tabby kitten was found in the streets by a Good Samaritan and brought to Cincinnati Animal Care, where he was diagnosed with a spinal injury.

While not paralyzed, his little back limbs had atrophied from lack of use, and he needed a way to get around while regaining his muscle strength. But none of the devices at the shelter were a good fit.

"He was only about just shy of one pound when he came," Mallory Smith, veterinary assistant lead at Cincinnati Animal Care, told As It Happens guest host Rebecca Zandbergen. "He was a really little guy."

So Smith, who is currently fostering said little guy, decided to get creative and make one herself out of household items, including Hot Wheels, zip ties, and lots and lots of duct tape.

"When a tiny kitten comes in who needs some extra help getting around, you use what's available to make it happen," the shelter wrote in a social media post.

The key component? 99-cent rulers

Wheelchairs for cats and dogs aren't actually chairs, but rather harnesses that strap the animal to a set of back wheels, so they can use their front legs to pull themselves around.

It took some experimenting to get Gelato's just right, says Smith.

For her first prototype, she used cardboard to fashion a cradle and two legs. At the bottom of each leg she fastened a Hot Wheels ambulance. The whole contraption was held together with zip ties and electrical tape.

But the cardboard didn't cut it.

"They weren't able to hold up his weight, especially when he would try and turn. So then I just got some wooden rulers for 99 cents each and put them on the sides."

Thus, Gelato's chariot was born.

Gelato suffered a spinal injury that made his hind legs give out, but he is slowly regaining his muscle strength and shelter staff expect him to make a full recovery. (Submitted by Mallory Smith)

"He was able to walk around with it and it gave him some autonomy while also getting physical therapy at the same time," she said.

Out with the Hot Wheels, in with the actual wheels

Smith says the device soon turned Gelato into an internet celebrity. But despite its charm, she says it wasn't a good long-term solution for the growing kitten.

She has since worked with an engineer friend to design Gelato a 3D-printed wheelchair that's adjustable as he grows.

"He's able to use it really well and it's very exciting," she said.

Gelato uses his device to get around and play, while undergoing regular physiotherapy to get his back legs moving again.

So far, Smith says, he's showing progress.

"He's already starting to stand up on his own without the wheelchair assistance, but he can't quite take a lot of steps," she said. "But I have a good feeling that he will be able to walk unassisted soon enough."

Gelato eventually swapped his duct-tape wheelchair for an adjustable 3D-printed one. (Submitted by Mallory Smith)

Smith says she's glad Gelato is bringing attention to the need for a wider variety of assisted mobile devices for animals.

"There's definitely other kittens who are in need of this stuff," she said. "I'm really happy that he's getting that attention to kind of broadcast a bigger light on special needs animals in general."

If all goes well, he will walk right into a new home as soon as he's ready for adoption. It'll be a bittersweet moment for Smith, who has grown fond of her little ward.

"I do really, really love him, but if I were to keep him, then it would hinder my ability to help the next animal that needs a foster," she said.

She doesn't think it'll take for Gelato to get scooped up.

"He's a popular guy."

World.title: Lloyd Robertson dead at 92: Peers and friends pay tribute to iconic broadcaster's career
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Lloyd Robertson, who delivered the news to Canadians in an authoritative and unflappable manner for more than 40 years as anchor for the flagship news programs of CTV and CBC, has died. He was 92.

His death was first reported by CTV and was confirmed by a family member to CBC News.

Robertson stepped away as CTV National News anchor in 2011 after 35 years, having joined the network in a move from CBC that reshaped Canadian broadcast news. He had been anchor of CBC's The National for six years.

"Someone came along with this … on my terms, in my life at precisely the right moment, and it was irresistible. I couldn't turn it down," he told CBC's Take 30 in 1976, days after accepting the offer.

At CTV, Robertson helped lead coverage of 11 federal elections, three Canadian-hosted Olympic Games and two Quebec referendums, as well as tragedies like the 1985 Air India bombing, 1989 Montreal massacre and the Sept. 11 attacks. He also helped share inspiring stories such as Terry Fox's Marathon of Hope.

WATCH | Robertson announces retirement: Lloyd Robertson retires | Duration 3:50 CTV anchor stepping down after decades-long career, including 22 years at CBC

Robertson frequently spoke of enjoying being at the centre of attention for events shaping Canada and the world, but his on-air style was once accurately described as "self-effacing and lacking in the watch-me swagger of most news anchors," by Globe and Mail television critic John Doyle.

Robertson was "the guy with the smallest ego I've ever seen in the television business, when he has a right to the largest one," Henry Kowalski, former CTV news chief, told the same newspaper in 2001.

"He was not just a fine journalist but a fine person," said Peter Mansbridge, former chief correspondent for CBC News, describing Robertson as a "friend and colleague of mine for more than 50 years.

"His audience believed him, and they trusted him. He set the bar for those who anchored newscasts across the country, and he will always be remembered for that.”

In addition to a number of industry awards during his career, he was inducted as an officer into the Order of Canada in 1997 and into the Canadian News Hall of Fame for the Canadian Journalism Foundation in 2016.

"If you find something that you love to do, and you're able to do it, that's about as good as it gets in life," Robertson said in a 2012 CTV documentary And That's the Life I Led.

WATCH | Robertson reports on new skateboarding fad in 1965: The scoop on 'skurfing' | Duration 2:19 The teenage president of the Ontario branch of the National Sidewalk Surfers of Canada explains her organization's reason for being.

Robertson was born in Stratford, Ont., on Jan. 19, 1934, to parents George and Lilly, the youngest of their two children by nine years. He also had eight older half-siblings from the first marriage of his father, whose ancestors emigrated from Scotland in the mid-19th century.

He hung on the advice and political musings of his father, a Canadian National Railway machinist, and the pair enjoyed radio comedies together.

But it was often a "dreary home life," he wrote in his 2012 memoir The Kind of Life It's Been, owing to his British mother's struggles with mental illness. Prone to bouts of paranoia and obsessive-compulsive behaviour, she would be lobotomized when he was 14, quelling her mind to a degree but dulling her emotional connection with her son.

"I couldn't have kids to the house, I couldn't tell them about her," he told CBC's George Stroumboulopoulos Tonight in 2012.

High school classmates, in the 2012 CTV documentary that accompanied his memoir, remembered a friend who gave little sign of turmoil. Robertson was popular, participating in debate and a barbershop quartet at Stratford Central Secondary School.

WATCH | Lisa LaFlamme on Robertson's legacy: ‘My life changed because of Lloyd Robertson’: Lisa LaFlamme reflects on the passing of her mentor | Duration 9:50 Former CTV National News anchor Lisa LaFlamme reflects on the passing of her friend and mentor, Lloyd Robertson, who has died at age 92. LaFlamme remembers Robertson’s belief in her during her time at CTV News, his dedication to fairness and humanity in news, and how he shaped her life beyond the newsroom.

22-year run at CBC

Already gifted with a smooth voice, he'd been intrigued by radio after standing near reporters covering a post-war parade in his hometown in 1946.

"I just remember being fascinated by the voices of the two commentators as they painted vivid pictures of the marchers and the joyous crowds," he wrote in his memoir.

At just 17, he persuaded Stratford radio station CJCS to give him an opportunity, overcoming an early on-air bungled pronunciation of the city name as "Strat-herd."

He didn't consider going beyond high school, learning the craft of radio at private stations in Stratford and Guelph, before beginning a 22-year run with the public broadcaster in 1954 in Windsor.

WATCH | Robertson anchors CBC in 1970: Lloyd Robertson, rookie news anchor | Duration 1:43 Lloyd Robertson was an anchor at the CBC before he became the face of CTV News.

For Robertson, 1956 was a momentous year — his elderly father died just months after he landed at CBC Winnipeg for his first foray into television.

That year he also married Nancy Barrett, a high school sweetheart with whom he had remained in touch. The couple would welcome four daughters born in Winnipeg, Ottawa and Toronto, reflecting Robertson's peripatetic, upward climb.

In his memoir, he remembered his four-plus years in Winnipeg as "among my happiest and most productive," and he even donned Western garb to host the country-flavoured Saddle Songs. He then honed political chops with a two-year stint with CBC Ottawa — though it wasn't all Parliament Hill business, as he hosted a show about the CFL's Ottawa Rough Riders.

WATCH | Mansbridge on how Robertson 'changed the nature' of TV news in Canada: Lloyd Robertson, veteran news anchor, dead at 92 | Duration 10:43 Celebrated Canadian news anchor Lloyd Robertson has died at age 92. The veteran journalist began his career in local radio in 1952 before joining the CBC as an announcer in 1956. Robertson moved to CTV National News in 1976, serving as co-anchor and later chief anchor until his retirement in 2011. Former CBC News chief correspondent Peter Mansbridge shares his memories of Lloyd.

In 1962 came an offer from the corporation the couple couldn't refuse, and another move. Robertson would remember being at the "bottom of the pile" of 30 announcers, all male, at CBC Toronto.

Robertson would separate himself over time, displaying adaptability by hosting a kid's show, the athletics program Kaleidosport, and a host of news and magazine programs. Many Canadian radio listeners first heard of John F. Kennedy's assassination in 1963 from Robertson, and he would score high-profile network assignments for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and Expo '67 in Montreal.

Robertson was cool and collected on air, but admitted years later that co-anchoring the 1969 moon shot by U.S. astronauts gave him pause.

"I had to pinch myself to be sure I was really living through this momentous time," he wrote.

Robertson would be rewarded with the network's plum assignment of anchoring The National in late 1970. It was a baptism by fire, as within days the Front de libération du Québec would plunge the province and country into crisis, kidnapping British diplomat James Cross and ultimately killing provincial minister Pierre Laporte.

CBC's news and current affairs roster was deep in the first years of that decade — future Canadian news anchors Peter Kent, Peter Trueman, Peter Mansbridge and Jan Tennant, along with budding stars like Adrienne Clarkson, Barbara Frum and Alex Trebek.

But there were also increasingly outdated union strictures involving studio and field work. Robertson once shared his workplace frustrations with Walter Cronkite on a trip to U.S. He recounted that the CBS news titan was incredulous that CBC anchors couldn't write their own copy, and were limited in reporting outside of the studio.

Move to CTV

In a time where NBC and ABC were employing multi-anchor formats in the U.S., Robertson was promised more freedom upon joining CTV National News in 1976, even as Harvey Kirck remained on the desk.

"Life with Harvey was sometimes tumultuous, occasionally precarious, but never dull," he wrote in his memoir of a co-anchor he described as loyal, but who caused the news division headaches with impaired driving citations.

Robertson adjusted to private-sector reality — more commercials, and local affiliates with clout — but he was welcomed by colleagues.

WATCH | Robertson on why he moved to CTV: Career change for Lloyd Robertson | Duration 1:39 The CBC's Larry Stout learns why money wasn't the only thing that motivated Lloyd Robertson to leave CBC for CTV. Aired on CBC's The National on June 21, 1976.

"What Lloyd did is [he] gave us instant credibility, and our numbers began to climb, and we've never retreated, really," said Craig Oliver, a top CTV political reporter and off-air friend, in 2012.

Kirck's departure in 1984 established Robertson's pre-eminence. Around the same time, coincidentally, he was approached by the Conservative Party to run as an MP. He wrote years the prospect held "some appeal," but he rebuffed that entreaty, and one by the Liberal Party in the early 2000s to serve as a senator.

By the 1990s, Roberton was ending the newscast with what would become a trademark: "And that's the kind of day it's been." He was firmly established as an éminence grise in the industry, winning three Geminis that decade for best host, anchor or interviewer.

Robertson stands with his star at Canada's Walk of Fame in Toronto in June 2007. (Mark Blinch/Reuters)

Robertson initiated a plan to step back from anchoring in 1996 and give way to CTV reporter Keith Morrison, but, he wrote years later, it imploded due to a combination of corporate resistance and misunderstandings. He expressed regret that the personal relationship with Morrison was ruptured beyond repair.

Robertson would still be in the anchor chair in the next decade and beyond, pulling a 14-hour shift on Sept. 11, 2001, the day of the terrorist attacks on U.S. soil by Islamist militants.

"The magnitude of this crisis is truly breathtaking," he told viewers. He admitted to The Canadian Press that days later his voice "may have been trembling a little bit," describing the scene as tens of thousands who had gathered on Parliament Hill for several minutes of silence in honour of what would be nearly 3,000 innocent victims, including 24 Canadians.

PHOTOS | Robertson through the years:

Robertson tributes flowed in 2010, and the year after, as he gave a year's notice of his intention to leave the anchor post.

"I've never seen Lloyd angry," Kent, then a federal politician, marvelled at the time. "Lloyd is a gentleman and a paragon of integrity."

Robertson remained with the network for several more years, contributing to investigative program W5, and he continued charitable work that included raising awareness of mental illness.

He was able to spend more time with his children and grandchildren, who were used to that sometimes-booming baritone.

"There's a line that we use: 'Dad, I'm in the room,'" daughter Susan Robertson told CTV in 2012. "But that's his trademark, that's his voice."

While straight-laced on air, Robertson wasn't overly fussy with his image, appearing in comedic skits with the Royal Canadian Air Farce, and with Drake in a taped segment for the Juno Awards. As to SCTV's newscaster "Floyd Robertson," he told CBC he thought the portrayal by Joe Flaherty was "marvelous."

World.title: Heated Rivalry cast and crew need space while shooting Season 2, director says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Attention Heated Rivlary fans: There are no smoothies for you at the Straw + Berry. This is not your ice time. And no, you can't come to the cottage.

At least not until Season 2 of Heated Rivalry is done filming.

Director Jacob Tierney has posted a gentle request for space for the cast and crew of the beloved television series while they film Season 2. It was also posted on the show's official Instagram account.

The message was addressed to the show's "incredible fans" and said, "if you happen to come across one of our filming locations, please give our cast and crew the space they need to do what they do best."

Heated Rivalry Season 2 is being filmed primarily in Toronto and Montreal, according to the industry website Production List, and the crew may also return to some familiar sites in Hamilton, Ont.

But fans have already proved they are eager to catch a glimpse of the show's stars Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie.

They were seen walking together in downtown Toronto over the weekend, and even inspired some frenzied shopping trips to Canadian Tire after Williams was photographed carrying one of the store's reusable bags.

WATCH | Hudson Williams causes frenzy over Canadian Tire tote bag: Why Canadian Tire's tote bag is having a moment | Duration 1:15 Canadian Tire tote bags are causing a frenzy online, all because actor Hudson Williams was seen with one on his arm.

When the queer hockey romance premiered in late 2025, it scored Williams and Storrie legions of fans around the world, earning them a level of attention rarely experienced by the stars of Canadian TV shows.

Since then, the actors have been careful to draw boundaries with fans and paparazzi alike.

Over the weekend, the celebrity gossip site Deux Moi shared comments from one person who claimed to have approached Storrie in Toronto, only to be told, "sorry, I'm not doing photos right now."

Last month, Williams was recorded during a tense confrontation with alleged autograph-sellers in Paris who apparently followed him and his entourage to the place they were staying.

Heated Rivalry is not the only set with a high-profile actor drawing attention in Toronto right now.

Sarah Polley's movie adaptation of The Bell Jar features pop star Billie Eilish, and it is supposed to have a closed set, but that didn't stop photos from cropping up on social media over the weekend.

Some appeared to be close-ups taken by paparazzi with long-range lenses and sold to the celebrity news agency Backgrid. Others appear to be taken by fans and passers-by.



So far, neither the director nor the film's official Instagram account have gone so far as to put out a public request for space.

World.title: Filipino tennis star Alex Eala riding a wave of popularity into Toronto tournament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When rising Filipino tennis star Alex Eala plays on Canadian soil at the National Bank Open in Toronto, she'll be on centre court in front of a sold out crowd of 10,000.

The moment Eala's appearance was announced — a second round Wednesday night match — seats sold out within 30 minutes, according to Karl Hale, tournament director for the NBO, Canada's biggest tennis tournament and one of the most prestigious on the WTA tour.

"We've never seen a player ranked outside the top five have this type of effect," Hale said. "I think her fans were specifically waiting to see when she played."

And it's not just happening in Toronto.

The WTA tour is a gruelling season of more than 50 tournaments across dozens of countries, spanning multiple continents. And with every appearance, Eala's fans seem to find her.

"All the tournament directors are talking about it, everybody in the industry is talking about it," said Hale.

Eala's popularity has been driven by a massive Filipino diaspora, but also the vitality of her dramatic wins and charismatic interviews. She's a fresh face on the tour that has looked for star power following the retirement of big names like Serena Williams.

Eala kisses the championship trophy after winning the women's singles championship match at the Mubadala D.C. Open 2026, making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title. (Scott Taetsch/Getty Images)

But with that growing popularity has come some backlash, with some online critics calling her overhyped.

However, Eala will play in Toronto fresh off a historic win at the Mubadala D.C. Open in Washington, D.C., making her the first tennis player from the Philippines to bag a WTA title.

"She's now 20 in the world. So she is really backing it up and she's growing her fan base," said Hale.

Big crowds at all tournaments

The early seeds of that fandom came when Eala reached the semifinals of another prestigious WTA tournament in 2025, the Miami Open. She beat out big names, including two top five players.

From there, the crowds only got bigger, extending even to the Grand Slams — the four biggest tournaments of the tennis season.

At last year's U.S. Open in New York, an energized crowd gave her first-round match the feel of a more consequential clash. Eala came from behind to win, marking the first time a player from the Philippines won a Grand Slam match.

From there, the so-called Eala effect seemed to catch.

Fans lined up for hours to catch her in the first round of this year's Australian Open in Melbourne. At the time, Eala was ranked 49th and lost that first match.

Her fans carried flags, signs and cheered so loud, it was noted by the opponent who beat her, American Alycia Parks.

After the match, Parks said, "It was difficult," mentioning that Eala definitely had a good crowd.

Then at Wimbledon in London, the crowd roared when she upset the defending champ Iga Swiatek in the third round.

"It is incredible to have my countrymen cheering me on, knowing that we are all in this together," Eala said in the post-match interview .

American tennis star turned-podcaster Andy Roddick has called it "Eala-mania."

On his podcast, he said: "Eala-mania is fun! When you have watch parties in arenas around your country for a fourth-round match, I'm in."

A new kind of tennis star

Eala's popularity signals a shift in tennis that many have long called for — more diversity.

The top-ranked players in the sport are concentrated in North America and Europe, with the dominant clusters in the U.S., Russia, Spain and France.

Asia has had few players break through the top ranks, while the Philippines, a country of 100 million people, has never produced a tennis star before.

Eala has noted this, embracing her Filipino fans and speaking in her native tongue often during her tournament interviews.

Alex Eala serves in a match at the U.S. Open in New York City in August 2025. (Kris Reyes/CBC)

As a Filipino Canadian tennis fan, I can speak to that pride. My whole family has been following Eala since she won the junior's girls title at the U.S. Open in 2022, excited at the prospect of cheering for another Filipino in a sport we already loved.

And there is a kind of thrill, hearing words like laban, the Tagalog word for fight, shouted from the stands at international tournaments.

It is a joy to watch an entire country, the Filipino diaspora and the rest of the tennis world get excited to walk alongside Eala in pursuit of bigger titles, even a Grand Slam trophy.

Eala's rise has put her on the cover of every major publication in her country, from Vogue to Tatler, while garnering congratulations from Filipinos everywhere in the world, including the Philippine president.

"Everywhere around the world, we have been watching you. We've been willing you on, and we have been so proud of you," President Bongbong Marcos said at a reception hosted for the athlete at the nation's presidential palace.

She's credited the love and support of her country for motivating her to continue battling on the court.

In an interview in 2022 with the WTA , she explained why she considers it a privilege to be a banner holder for the Philippines.

"It's important to me because I don't see a lot of Filipinos on the worldwide tennis stage."

World.title: The next Toronto? Reports of urban raccoons on the rise in Calgary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sean Halvorsen never thought he would be sharing his house with a raccoon.

That changed about a month ago, when his son caught a glimpse of a black-and-white bandit atop their McKenzie Lake home.

"All of a sudden the cat freaked out and my son looked out and saw what he thought was a cat, but it was actually a raccoon on the roof," he said.

"That's where I first realized I might have a raccoon problem."

Raccoons are seldom seen in most of Alberta, where harsh winters and abundant predators are among the challenges they've faced.
