World.title: Fears of renewed conflict in Ethiopia
World.content:
Military activity in and around the disputed city of Alamata has sparked concerns that the fragile peace that followed the 2020–2022 Tigray War could unravel.

Residents of Alamata, a city that straddles Ethiopia's Tigray and Amhara regions. say a growing military presence have them fearing renewed fighting.

The city is one of the most contested areas since the Tigray War. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) forces took control of it at the start of this year, after Ethiopian federal troops withdrew.

One Alamata resident who requested anonymity for safety reasons said: "The TPLF forces have deployed many troops on the Raya front and have been instructed to be ready for war."

"In most areas of the city, you can only see soldiers," another Alamata resident, Ato Gebru TsefaEzigi, told DW. "It seems like a military city."

Alamata is the central hub of the Raya valley, which straddles the Tigray and Amhara regions and alongside. It includes the districts of Raya Azebo in the Tigray region and Raya Kobo in the Amhara region.

Explainer: How did Ethiopia's Tigray war start? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Did Ethiopia forces strike in Western Tigray?

In a statement on August 2, the regional government in Tigray said its forces had repelled an "open military offensive against the Tigray Security Forces in the vicinity of Shererina, Western Tigray" by Ethiopian federal forces.

It also stated that the federal forces were supported by forces belonging to Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). DW could not independently verify the claims.

The Ethiopian federal government has not responded to the Tigray government's statement. However, Ethiopian media reported that Abraham Belay, the federal Minister of Irrigation and Lowland Areas acknowledged that clashes had taken place in western Tigray and blamed the TPLF for intitiating them.

A highly contested area

Alamata lies about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of Kobo in the Amhara region and sits along a strategic highway linking Tigray with central Ethiopia.

Ethiopian federal forces entered the city in November 2020, at the start of the Tigray War. Forces loyal to the TPLF and deployed TPLF army units have been in control since federal forces withdrew on January 15.

However, the area's status remains unresolved under the African Union-brokered Pretoria Peace Agreement signed in November 2022. Political divisions within the TPLF have also fueled concerns about the durability of the peace process.

An estimated 600,000 people died in the 2020-2022 war. Millions were displaced and essential services collapsed across Tigray and much of northern Ethiopia. The federal government and the TPLF accused each other of having initiated the conflict.

Calls for access and restraint

Although the Pretoria agreement largely ended large-scale fighting, several key provisions remain unimplemented, including the status of disputed areas and the restoration of civilian administration in some of them.

The African Union has repeatedly urged all parties to fully implement the Pretoria agreement and resolve disputes through dialogue. Human rights group Amnesty International has also called for restraint and renewed its calls for independent access to the conflict-affected areas.

"We are also calling for access for human rights observers, investigators, and journalists to Tigray and to all regions impacted by the conflict in Ethiopia," said Suad Nur, Amnesty's Horn of Africa campaigner. "Because we know what happens when perpetrators commit crimes or conduct hostilities where there is no scrutiny or oversight ... We know what happens when hostilities unfold without scrutiny or oversight."

The new crisis facing Tigray’s families To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regional implications

Renewed instability in northern Ethiopia could have consequences beyond the country's borders. International humanitarian agencies are currently overstretched in countries like Sudan and Somalia.

Analysts warn that renewed fighting in and around Tigray could trigger the displacement of even more people, disrupt trade routes and complicate peace efforts in the region.

For Alamata residents and those in Ethiopian communities still recovering from one of Africa's deadliest conflicts, the latest military movements have revived painful memories of conflict.

World.title: India's Gen Z protest enters a new online battle
World.content:
The streets are quiet, but a fight over the legacy of the Cockroach Janta Party movement is intensifying across Instagram, memes and social media.

The crowds have long dispersed from the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) main New Delhi protest site next to the Jantar Mantar.

But the CJP's 36-day campaign, which started as a satirical protest against exam leaks and grew into a wider movement voicing young Indians' anger over jobs and education, has entered a new phase.

The authorities and the CJP are now battling to shape how India's first Gen Z-led protest will be remembered.

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on July 25, fulfilling one of the CJP's key demands after weeks of protests that withstood tear gas and baton charges.

India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) says the minister's resignation demonstrates government accountability, while the CJP argues it was a concession won through sustained public pressure.

The BJP has mounted a coordinated online campaign aimed at reframing the movement, observers say.

Government ministers and CJP leaders shook hands at a press conference in Delhi, seemingly declaring a truce of sorts Image: ANI

MPs Bansuri Swaraj and Sambit Patra have shared videos of protesters allegedly abusing Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his late mother, while Modi himself said he forgave those responsible.

Meanwhile, BJP leaders J P Nadda and Pradhan have argued that opposition parties and "anti-national forces" sought to exploit genuine student grievances for political gain.

BJP spokesperson Shazia Ilmi rejects suggestions that the party is trying to divert attention from education reform.

"A generation capable of reinventing political communication through memes and satire should not have fallen back on crude abuse," Ilmi told DW, referring to slogans directed at Modi and his late mother.

The meme war

CJP supporters tell a very different story.

Instead of lengthy political rebuttals, they have continued to flood Instagram with memes, parody reels and remix videos that mock the BJP's attempts to appear youthful, while insisting the central issue remains education reform and accountability.

Modi said the language used by some protesters 'would not suit any civilized society' Image: Sajjad Hussain/AFP

Apar Gupta, founding director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, believes the Cockroach movement exposed a generational shift in political communication.

Gupta said that the BJP's digital strategy was designed for the WhatsApp era.

"Instagram is a different ecosystem," he told DW. "It rewards authenticity, personal storytelling and virality, allowing Gen Z creators to set the terms of debate before official narratives can catch up."

"Gen Z may have won the cultural conversation through reels, memes and satire, but the state still retains institutional power through takedown requests, digital surveillance and investigations," Gupta said.

"The battle is no longer just over public opinion; it is over how the protests will be remembered."

CJP creators frequently juxtapose government announcements with unemployment statistics, canceled exams and footage from the protests.

When BJP leaders adopted Gen Z slang on party-linked accounts, students responded with satire, portraying the outreach as awkward and performative rather than authentic.

Some of the movement's most widely shared content relied on humor rather than slogans.

"Get Ready With Me" videos showing students padding their clothes before facing police batons, clips filmed inside police vans and self-deprecating memes about arrests kept the movement alive online long after the tents at Jantar Mantar were dismantled.

For Neha Bora, president of the All-India Students' Association (AISA), the government's response follows a familiar script.

"This is nothing new," she told DW. "They are attempting to shrink what was a broad-based student movement into a communal story because that serves their political agenda."

Instagram changes the rules

For years, the BJP set the pace of India's online political conversation.

Cockroach revolution turns on India's leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Modi's 2014 campaign, widely described as India's first "Twitter election," transformed social media into a powerful electoral tool.

The Cockroach movement suggested that model may no longer be sufficient.

Questions about digital power extended beyond political parties, however, when Meta temporarily removed one of Modi's videos during the protests before restoring it and apologizing, attributing the removal to an automated moderation error.

For the BJP, the episode became evidence that global technology platforms were actively shaping political narratives.

Senior leaders, including Nishikant Dubey, chairman of Parliament's Standing Committee on Communications and IT, questioned Meta's actions after Modi's video was briefly removed, saying it raised "serious questions" about the platform's intent.

Beyond the hashtags

Media commentator Pamela Philipose, who researches social media and social movements, believes it was inevitable that attention would eventually move beyond the demonstrations themselves.

But she argues that would represent a failure if the underlying questions disappear with the hashtags.

"The real issue is whether India can build an education system that offers fairness, credibility and opportunity to millions of young people," Philipose told DW. "Reforming examinations is only one part of that larger democratic challenge."

Philipose emphasizes that the CJP's real achievement was not simply forcing a ministerial resignation but enabling young people to tell their own story without relying on traditional media.

Gupta argues that, regardless of who wins today's narrative battle, something more fundamental has changed.

"A generation that treats the internet as its civic square, and defends it with wit, is India's constitutional guarantee of free speech working as intended," he said.

Whether the BJP succeeds in reclaiming the narrative or the CJP keeps the focus on education reform remains uncertain. What is already clear is that India's first digital-native protest did not end when the tents came down at Jantar Mantar.

It has simply moved online, where reels, memes and competing political narratives are shaping how the movement will be remembered.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Middle East: Israel strikes southern Lebanon, accuses Hezbollah of 'blatant' ceasefire violation
World.content:
08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 UN 'alarmed' by frequent executions in Iran

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has warned of an increase in executions and death sentences in Iran this year,

Volker Türk said that at least 56 people had been executed in Iran on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 cases linked to the protests at the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran.

"I am alarmed by the rise in executions and death sentences issued in Iran since March, and that capital punishment continues to be used to instill fear among the population and suppress dissent," Türk said in a statement.

Türk said more than 100 further people were at risk of the death penalty based on similar security-related charges, and also said executions for drug-related offenses were becoming more common.

As recently as Monday of this week, Iran's judiciary said that two men had been executed on charges of spying for Israel during the 12-day war between the two countries last summer.

Iran was already one of the most prolific users of the death penalty on the planet prior to this year's domestic and international conflict.

In the countries tracked by Amnesty International, Iran, a country of some 93 million people, was logged as committing 2,159 or more executions last year, or six times as many as its regional rival Saudi Arabia, with its population of 35 million.

World.title: Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament
World.content:
On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.

Japan on Thursday commemorates the 81st anniversary of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima.

On August 6, 1945, the US dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima during the last days of World War II, killing close to 80,000 people in the initial blast. Three days later, the US dropped a bomb over Nagasaki.

"Japan adopted a pacifist constitution in reflection on World War II," noted Masako Wada, assistant secretary general of Nihon Hidankyo, or the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers' Organizations.

Japan "earned the trust of the international community as a country that promised never to wage a war again," added Wada, who survived the Nagasaki bombing as a 1-year-old.

The dropping of the atomic bomb on August 6, 1945, flattened more than two-thirds of Hiroshima [FILE: September 8, 1945] Image: Stanley Troutman/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, in recent years, Japan has increased defense spending, eased restrictions on weapons exports and expanded the role of its military, citing growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia.

"The current administration is destroying that [trust]," Wada told DW, referring to Japan's recent efforts to pivot away from decades of strict postwar pacifism.

"Japan's recent military buildup is no different from recreating the arms race that led the country toward World War II," said 84-year-old Masashi Ieshima, who survived the Hiroshima bombing at the age of 3.

Survivors warn against rearmament

Ieshima was playing in the entrance of his house, just 1.2 miles (2 km) from the hypocenter, when the blast shattered all the windows in the house, sending shards of glass into his mother.

Hiroshima 'successors' keep telling atomic bomb stories To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Seventy years later, he underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, which was officially recognized as an atomic bomb-related illness. His father, who was also exposed to the Hiroshima atomic bombing, died of laryngeal cancer.

"It makes my blood boil to see Japan justify its military buildup and the easing of arms export restrictions over the possibility of a Taiwan conflict," said Ieshima, who serves as the chairman of Toyukai, the Tokyo affiliate of Nihon Hidankyo.

"If Japan continues down this path, it could lead to war. And if another war breaks out, I believe it will be a nuclear war."

The average age of Japan's atomic bomb survivors, known as "hibakusha," has reached almost 87. They face the urgent challenge of passing on their testimony and calls for peace to younger generations, including their children, grandchildren, and supporters.

Takako Nakamura, a second-generation atomic bomb survivor from Nagasaki, began working actively as a family testimony speaker in February 2026, following her career retirement.

"People were killed without a trace, not even their bones remain. That is the true nature of the atomic bomb," the 73-year-old told DW, her voice breaking.

Wada urged people around the world to recognize that the danger of nuclear weapons is "not something in the past, but in front of us right now."

She said she does not want sympathy for survivors, but empathy. "I want people to think of it as their own issue."

Japan pushes for military buildup, non-nuclear principles at risk

On Tuesday, Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the country needs to strengthen its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis" as a new government assessment again highlighted growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

In the preface to Japan's latest annual defense white paper , Koizumi said it was "imperative that Japan further reinforce and transform its defense capabilities with a stronger sense of urgency and crisis than ever before."

An atomic bomb explodes after being dropped by a US Air Force B-29 bomber over Nagasaki [FILE: August 9, 1945] Image: U.S. Army Air Forces/Library of Congress/REUTERS

The Defense Ministry told DW that Japan must strengthen its defense capabilities to enhance deterrence while maintaining its exclusively defense-oriented policy.

It cited an increasingly severe security environment, including China's military expansion and activities in the East and South China seas and around Taiwan.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has introduced a series of measures to strengthen Japan's defense capabilities. Her

Her government also relaxed restrictions on arms exports in April 2026, allowing exports of lethal weapons.

It is also considering revising Japan's long-standing commitment to the three non-nuclear principles of not possessing, producing or permitting the entry of nuclear weapons onto Japanese territory.

In November 2025, Takaichi said that a Chinese military attack on Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its legal right to collective self-defense.

Many Japanese Gen Zers are opposed to Japan's military expansion Image: Daiki Tateyama/DW

However, the argument that Japan must strengthen its military because China might invade Japan or Taiwan is "not convincing" to the Japanese public, said Koichi Nakano, a professor of political science at Sophia University in Tokyo.

China's military activities, including its maritime expansion, remain limited compared with Russia's war in Ukraine and US attacks on Iran, he told DW.

"Japan is being skillfully drawn into the narrative that it must fall into line with Europe and the US to confront so-called rogue states such as China, North Korea and Russia."

"Japan must responsibly pursue disarmament and establish dialogue," Nakano said. "It must stop demonizing China and recognize it as a country with which meaningful dialogue is possible."

Youth in Japan take to the streets in anti-war protests

Meanwhile, around 27,000 people gathered on July 10 outside the Japanese parliament building in Tokyo, holding colorful illustrated placards with messages such as "No war," and waving glow sticks in the dark.

Reina Tashiro, 36, a member of a civil organization "We Want Our Future," told DW that they aim to "make it as easy as possible for people to take that first step and join a protest."

"It is different from the traditional image of demonstrations, where people raise their fists and shout slogans," Tashiro added. "Our protests may even look stylish."

Nahoko Hishiyama, who has been involved in civic activism for 24 years since the age of 13 and now serves as co-chair of another activist group, pointed out that recent protests have increasingly been led by people in their 20s to 40s, and more women are taking part.

"Japanese women are often said to be too mindful of how others perceive them. In activism, however, that has been turned into a strength, thinking about how to present our message in a way that resonates with the public."

Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: A glowing future for nuclear power? Mini reactors explained
World.content:
Mini reactors are seen as a flexible energy source. Their promise: abundant energy, cheap, clean and climate-friendly with lower water use. But do the numbers add up? We look at what's behind the SMR hype.

Many politicians and tech companies are now pushing to build new nuclear power plants to meet the world's rapidly growing energy demands. Small reactors — known as Small Modular Reactors, or SMRs — are gaining momentum.

They could be built in less time and come online faster than conventional nuclear power plants. Originally developed to power submarines and aircraft carriers, SMRs largely work the same way as larger reactors.

They contain a nuclear reactor fueled by uranium, which releases enormous amounts of heat through nuclear fission. That heat turns water into steam, and the steam pressure drives turbines that generate electricity.

Companies and startups are working on a wide variety of SMR designs and concepts, but the underlying principle is similar across all of them.

One advantage over conventional nuclear stations is that mini reactors require a maximum of two hectares (around five acres) of land — roughly the size of two soccer fields. By comparison, conventional plants require up to 280 soccer fields, according to the industry.

The Linglong One small modular pressurized water reactor after completing its factory test Image: Zhang Boqun/Xinhua/picture alliance

Why use a modular design for mini nuclear plants?

What makes SMRs particularly attractive is their modular construction. Individual components can be mass-produced as prefabricated modules and pre-assembled off-site — much like a prefab house that simply needs to be put together once it arrives at its location.

Manufacturers promise an extremely short construction time of between one and a half to six years. Large reactors in the US can take anywhere from seven to 10 years to build.

Proponents also argue that modular units could deliver low-emission power to remote regions, where grid infrastructure is often not developed enough to handle the enormous energy output of a large conventional plant.

Those advantages are also shared by renewable energy sources like solar panels and wind turbines — without the risks that come with nuclear power.

The hidden cost of nuclear power To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why less radiation can mean greater risk

The output of mini nuclear reactors is significantly lower than that of conventional nuclear power plants. Depending on the design, SMRs can deliver between 10 and around 200 megawatts of power, while a conventional plant generates between 1,000 and 1,600 MW.

To produce the same amount of energy as the roughly 400 high-capacity reactors currently operating worldwide, tens of thousands of small reactors would need to be built.

SMRs could offer some safety advantages: they contain less radioactive material than large reactors and would be distributed across multiple sites. This means that an accident or military strike resulting in a meltdown would not be as catastrophic as a worst-case scenario at a large reactor. Nevertheless, the consequences of an SMR accident could still be severe.

Germany's Federal Office for Radiation Protection points out that despite lower radiation levels per reactor, the overall risk posed by mini reactors could be many times higher. Replacing the output of existing nuclear plants with large numbers of smaller ones would require an enormous number of reactors worldwide — and that increases the likelihood that at least one of them will eventually suffer a serious incident.

Nuclear accidents and radiation leaks are extremely rare — but the consequences can be catastrophic. The last major nuclear accident occurred in 2011 at the Fukushima power plant in Japan, following a tsunami. Parts of the region have been contaminated for generations to come, and nearly 170,000 people were forced to flee their homes.

The core module of the Linglong One SMR being assembled at its construction site in Hainan Province, China Image: China National Nuclear Corporation/Handout via Xinhua/picture alliance

Extreme efficiency and the dream of radioactive recycling

Part of the hype around some new mini reactors rests on the hope of extracting significantly more energy from the same amount of uranium. Some SMR models — known as "fast reactors" — could theoretically yield 60 to 70 times more energy from uranium than conventional technology, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

But the technology is still in the early stages of development and has so far played only a limited role in IAEA projections. In practice, it has barely been proven in SMRs at all. Only two SMR facilities are currently in operation worldwide — one in China and one in Russia.

Work is also underway on recycling SMR fuel rods, but that process remains largely untested. Most SMR projects continue to rely on the same conventional technology used in traditional reactors.

And the problem of radioactive waste remains unsolved — for both conventional and fast reactors. The risks this poses are already visible: at the Asse facility in Lower Saxony, Germany, a temporary storage site built in the 1970s, hundreds of barrels of intermediate-level radioactive waste are now rusting and beginning to leak. Germany has yet to establish a permanent disposal site.

In fact, no permanent repository for spent fuel or highly radioactive reactor waste is currently in operation anywhere in the world. After 20 years of construction, the Onkalo facility in Finland is set to become the first when it opens in 2026.

Another problem for nuclear power is growing water scarcity. Recent heat and drought have already forced European nations to curb nuclear output due to for cooling due to low river levels.



Because SMRs are mainly just smaller, simplified versions conventional reactors, they still use water to run and for cooling. While individual units use less water than traditional plants, clustering units could increase overall use, warn experts. Researchers are investigating the use of alternative coolants like molten salts and helium gas for newer designs.

Underground tunnels of the Onkalo spent nuclear fuel repository in Finland, set to open in 2026 Image: Roni Rekomaa/Lehtikuva/dpa/picture alliance

When would SMRs make a climate impact — and at what cost?

Enthusiasm for small reactors runs high in the nuclear community. But what may look promising at first glance is, in many respects, difficult or impossible to back up with solid evidence.

Calculating the costs of a technology still in development is no easy task. Nevertheless, the German Institute for Economic Research estimates that electricity from new mini nuclear plants — even accounting for economies of scale, including construction and manufacturing — will cost at least twice as much per megawatt-hour as the already very affordable electricity generated by solar or wind power. In a worst-case scenario, the cost could be nearly eight times higher.

Adding up all the announcements, plans and strategies of major nations, a few hundred SMRs could come online in China, the US, Europe and India by 2050. But according to Germany's Federal Office for Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection, citing figures from the nuclear industry, production would only become economically viable at a threshold of 3,000 reactors.

The international community has committed to limiting global warmingto well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) by the end of the century. Meeting that target requires large parts of the global economy to become climate-neutral by 2050. The EU aims to reach zero emissions by then; Germany is even targeting net negative CO2 emissions by 2050.

That means climate-friendly nuclear technology would arrive too late to meaningfully limit global warming — and its advantages would be significantly diminished as a result.

What would remain: the radiation risk, and the question of what to do with the radioactive waste.

The toll of nuclear power on generations to come To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: My sleep deprivation is your natural short sleep
World.content:
Every so often we hear of high-ranking politicians or CEOs claiming to get by on very little sleep — some as little as three hours a night. If they’re not natural short sleepers, chances are they’re heading for trouble.

I've been having trouble sleeping — for as long as forever. Sometimes it's just a feeling. Other times, it's a fact (I know because my watch tells me). But then my watch may be part of the problem. It's constantly reminding me to get to bed on time and accosting me with poor sleep scores. It drives my anxiety through the roof, my heart races and I feel like I can't sleep. But then I still feel fine the next day. Weird.

"When you're sleep deprived, you have poor judgment," said Catia Reis, a sleep researcher at the University of Lisbon, when we spoke.

That might explain my predicament. Because even when I feel fine during the week, I oversleep at the weekend — which is a sure sign of sleep debt, she said.

Reis has studied a variety of sleep-related conditions, including the effects of jet lag and sleep deprivation among athletes.

One investigation compared levels of sleepiness among patients with sleep apnea — a condition where you stop breathing intermittently through the night — and shift workers, who work against their natural, circadian rhythm. That's our inner clock that tells us when we're wakeful or sleepy.

She compared the results from both subjective assessments made by participants and objective, clinical tests, and found a "mismatch" in people's ability to assess their own levels of sleepiness the more they were exposed to that very thing: sleepiness.

Basically, the brain stops working. And that should be concerning, given that the brain plays a central role in sleep.

Sleep or die

When we sleep, the body performs several restorative functions: It removes toxins we have ingested through food or the atmosphere, generates new energy, and is essential for our learning and memory.

"Sleep involves many parts of the brain," said Ying-Hui Fu, a sleep researcher at the University of California San Franscisco. "Almost every disease of the brain, including neurological and psychiatric, [can be linked to] sleep problems."

On average, people need about 7.5-8.5 hours' sleep per night.

But every so often we hear about people in demanding jobs, usually politicians, boasting — or claiming credibility — by saying they rarely sleep more than a few hours; like they're ALWAYS WORKING FOR THE PEOPLE.

Most recently, it was Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who reminded us she's slept between zero and three hours per night while in office.

As a former heavy metal drummer, you might expect a certain level of stamina from the Japanese PM. But while voluntary, habitual (or trained) sleep deprivation — if that's what it is in Takaichi's case — may be an impressive sleep-work-no-life-balance ethic, it's not a good, long-term strategy.

In the best-case scenario, a long-term "sleep debt" can cause your body to accumulate toxins, risking heart or brain disease. In the worst-case scenario, it can be fatal.

Why sleep is so important for your immune system To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"There are only two things more important than sleep for our total health," Fu told DW. "One is air. If we don't have air, we die in a few minutes. The other is water. If we don't have water, we die in a few days. If you don't eat, you can live a couple of months. But if you don't sleep, you can probably only live for a couple of weeks."

And that goes for all animals — "if we don't sleep, we die," she said.

The exception: natural short sleepers

Natural short sleepers are the exception to the rule. They can sleep fewer than six hours per night and not only feel fine, but also actually are fine — healthy, happy and energetic. They appear to have genetic variations that allow them to thrive. Fu cited an 80-year-old natural short sleeper who competed in triathlons.

Fu and her lab found the first of these variations in the gene DEC2 and published their findings in 2009. Ten years later, they published a paper suggesting that the gene ADRB1 was also linked to Natural Short Sleeper Syndrome. Findings into the genes NPSR1, GRM1, SIK3 followed, and there are others in the pipeline.

We're calling them gene "variations" rather than "mutations" because mutations are often associated with negative health effects. But it appears that Natural Short Sleep does not risk the health issues that habitual short sleepers or sleep deprived people face.

The genes show a range of functions that sleep effects:

DEC2: helps regulate sleep/wake duration

ADRB1: mediates cardiac and neuronal signaling

NPSR1: helps modulate arousal and anxiety

GRM1: involved in brain function; may be linked to depression

SIK3: plays a role in cell cycle-, metabolic and inflammatory- regulation

Each has taken years of painstaking basic — foundational — research to find and test.

"Every one of us has between 500 to 1,000 unique mutations in our genome. To know which one is causal is very difficult," said Fu.

Sleep smarter: How your body clock shapes your health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The impact of better sleep on humanity

The number of known natural short sleepers is small, but Fu says the condition is likely to be more common than research currently suggests.

Most of Fu's findings are limited families that share a gene variation. That's been for a practical, methodological reason: If three members of a family have the same variation and they all appear to be healthy on only four to six hours' sleep, then that gene variation may well be responsible, especially if it's in a gene that is known to be important for healthy sleep function. But it's early days.

"We just know that they perform better and they're healthier. And the most logical explanation for me is that their sleep function is better," said Fu.

Reis is also cautious about the state of research in this area, saying there are still too few studies into natural whort wleepers.

"When we objectively test [habitual short sleepers] and we expand their sleep, we know they improve," said Reis. "But the problem is we don't have enough longitudinal studies with [natural short sleepers]."

Fu would agree. But she said it was a struggle to get the research financed.

"My goal is to help everybody get good sleep. Because if we can help everybody get good sleep, all diseases will drop," said Fu. "The entire spectrum of disease incidence would drop. Can you imagine the impact on humanity?"

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: La Audiencia Nacional pregunta a la Guardia Civil si tuvo alguna información que pudiese “alertar” de la entrada masiva en Ceuta
World.content:
La Audiencia Nacional ha solicitado a la Guardia Civil que informe de si tuvo algún indicio o información en los días previos a la entrada irregular y masiva de inmigrantes en Ceuta que alertase de que lo sucedido podía ocurrir. La jueza María Tardón ha dado el paso a raíz de una denuncia del partido Iustitia Europa, que pide al tribunal que investigue los delitos “contra la seguridad del Estado, delitos contra la Nación, favorecimiento de la inmigración ilegal y tráfico de personas, organización criminal y omisión del deber de perseguir delitos”.

La cuestión de si hubo indicios o alertas previas que pudiesen haber preparado a los efectivos situados en la frontera, que fueron completamente superados, es una de las claves de esta crisis. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, insistía este miércoles en que el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI) no alertó de una llegada masiva de migrantes a Ceuta. Pero sí admitía que hubo avisos en los días previos de que, como es habitual en verano, podía haber “una ampliación, una elevación” del número de entradas irregulares por mar en la ciudad autónoma y de que en esta ocasión se podían “ver fomentadas” por la sentencia del Tribunal Supremo de comienzos de julio que prohibía las devoluciones en caliente de aquellas personas que entrasen a nado.

En una resolución judicial a la que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, la magistrada titular del Tribunal Central de Instancia número 3, María Tardón, solicita además a la Jefatura de Información del instituto armado que dé detalles sobre los días más críticos de la crisis migratoria —el 30 y el 31 de julio—, “particularmente en lo relativo a las operaciones de rescate de las personas que se hayan localizado en las aguas territoriales españolas, sus circunstancias personales conocidas, así como, en el caso de personas fallecidas, si constara la causa y la data de la muerte y, en el caso de las personas supervivientes, su identidad y datos de localización”.

Más información Playa de Trampolín: el refugio a sol abierto para centenares de subsaharianos que resisten en busca de asilo

El balance provisional de fallecidos es de 77. En las primeras horas, tras la entrada irregular de más de 70.000 personas del jueves, se recuperaron del mar 20 cuerpos. Al día siguiente fueron unos 40. Sus cuerpos se custodian ahora en un hangar refrigerado en el viejo hospital militar de la ciudad autónoma. Las autopsias casi están terminadas y se buscan formas de colaboración con Marruecos para identificar a los fallecidos.

No es la primera decisión de la instructora dentro de esta, de momento, incipiente causa: este martes, solicitó a la Policía Nacional un informe sobre la entrada “irregular masiva” de migrantes en Ceuta en los últimos días para dilucidar si se trató de “una acción concertada o dirigida” por algún “grupo criminal”. La solicitud busca establecer si la Audiencia Nacional es competente para investigar y más tarde juzgar los delitos denunciados por Iustitia Europa, partido que fue una de las acusaciones populares de, entre otros, el juicio al hermano de Pedro Sánchez y de la causa contra la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, Begoña Gómez.

Refuerzo del despliegue militar

En otra resolución conocida este miércoles, la jueza ha rechazado la solicitud planteada por Vox en su denuncia de reforzar bajo “supervisión judicial” el despliegue militar tanto en la frontera terrestre de la ciudad autónoma como en las aguas adyacentes a la misma. La jueza también descarta ordenar a la Policía y la Guardia Civil “intensificar” las identificaciones de personas en la vía pública al amparo de la ley de seguridad ciudadana, la conocida como ley mordaza. En su escrito, el partido de Santiago Abascal consideraba estas medidas urgentes “mientras persista la situación de riesgo” que considera que aún existe en Ceuta.

En su resolución, la magistrada señala que estas medidas son “ajenas al objeto y contenido del procedimiento penal” iniciado para esclarecer qué ocurrió con las víctimas y si las autoridades tenían información previa sobre lo que podía ocurrir. La magistrada añade que adoptarlas no son “competencia de ningún órgano judicial de instrucción” de la Audiencia Nacional. En la misma resolución, Tardón acuerda acumular en la causa abierta tanto la querella presentada por la organización ultracatólica Hazte Oír como la denuncia del partido de Santiago Abascal, y señala que esperará a recibir los informes solicitados tanto a la Policía Nacional como a la Guardia Civil sobre diferentes aspectos de lo ocurrido en la ciudad autónoma en los últimos días para resolver si la Audiencia Nacional es el órgano judicial competente para investigar los hechos, informa Óscar López-Fonseca.

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Dutch intelligence service ranked third best in Europe
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands has the third most highly rated intelligence service in Europe, according to a ranking published by the French magazine L’Express and based on a survey of intelligence professionals.

The AIVD, the Dutch civilian intelligence agency, ranked third after Britain’s MI6 and France’s DGSE. Ukraine’s SBU and HUR shared fourth place, followed by Germany’s BND.

The ranking is based on votes from 60 intelligence officials in 25 countries.

Huib Modderkolk, who covers intelligence for the Volkskrant, told broadcaster NOS the Dutch have especially strong technical capabilities.

The AIVD runs a joint cyber team with military intelligence agency MIVD whose work includes infiltrating Russian and Chinese systems, he said.

It also works closely with bigger partners, including the US, and increasingly with other European services, he said. One example is Estonia, a small country whose service deals heavily with Russia.

World.title: Jetten warns of rising hate at WorldPride conference
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has warned that hatred and intolerance against the LGBTQI+ community are growing, and that “hard-won progress” on equal rights is eroding around the world. He was speaking at the WorldPride Human Rights Conference in Amsterdam.

He said that many countries are backsliding on equal rights legislation and that homophobic hate speech is becoming more overt and aggressive. This is fuelled, he said, by “toxic, highly organised and well-funded groups hiding behind the façade of freedom of expression.”

He also referred to the Islamist attack at Berlin’s pride event on July 25, in which one person was killed and 29 injured. The suspect was later shot dead by police.

Jetten said despite the anger and sorrow, his “heart was filled with hope” when thousands gathered at Amsterdam’s Homomonument, the memorial to LGBTQI+ victims of persecution, days later in commemoration.

The prime minister’s speech was interrupted immediately after he took the stage as pro-Palestinian demonstrators began chanting “where is your red line” – referring to the protests against the Gaza war last year. One shouted “shame on you being at a human rights conference when you’re complicit in genocide.”

He responded as the protesters were being escorted out by asking the audience to give them a round of applause and describing the situation in Gaza and the West Bank as “horrific.”

Online hatred rising

Homophobia is spreading so rapidly because big social media companies are “barely moderating content for hate speech,” Jetten said.

Hate groups “no longer feel restrained,” he continued, “in my view, the rise of online hatred is one of the biggest threats facing LGBTQI+ people today… Misinformation – and disinformation – can be spread in the blink of an eye, with a single mouse-click.”

“Reaching much further than NGOs, youth workers and health organisations can.

This is always how hatred takes hold: In the shadows. Outside the spotlight of society. Underestimated by everyone.”

Funding and education initiatives

Over the next three years the government will invest €7.5 million annually in improving the safety of the queer community, Jetten said, and that a public information campaign will be launched to combat discrimination and disinformation.

Some of the money will fund Purple Friday, the day on which Dutch schools devote special attention to diversity, with pupils and teachers wearing purple to show their support. It has been run since 2010 by the GSA network of LGBTQI+ rights organisation COC and now involves thousands of primary and secondary schools.

The day has also become a point of contention. Surveys by NOS and RTL in 2024 found three-quarters of participating schools had run into problems, from posters being torn down to rainbow flags being set alight, and some had dropped it or rebranded it as a general “be yourself” day.

The conference comes 25 years after the Netherlands became the first country in the world to open marriage to same-sex couples. Four couples married at Amsterdam city hall a minute after midnight on April 1, 2001, and some 36,000 same-sex couples have married since.

World.title: Glasshouses feel cost of drought as sprinkler ban imposed
World.content:
Glasshouse operators in the Westland region could lose tens of millions of euros after a ban on sprinklers comes into force on Wednesday.

The glasshouse industry has not been exempted from the ban, which has been imposed by the Delfland water authority as an anti-drought measure.

All sluice gates in the region have been closed to protect drinking water from being contaminated by saltwater from the sea. Inspectors will check if companies are complying with the ban on using water for sprinkling.

“These measures are urgently needed to prevent irreversible damage happening,” a spokesman for the water board told Omroep West. “The glasshouse owners have been given until midnight [on Tuesday] to fill their reservoirs.”

Glastuinbouw Nederland, which represents the industry, said a two to three-week ban would cost companies around €150 million.

It has asked the water board if companies can spray their crops with purified waste water or seawater. “Almost any water is better than no water,” a spokesman said.

A ban on drawing water is also in force in parts of the Brabantse Delta region, around Breda. The ban, which initially covered the hours from 9am to 9pm, was extended last week to 24 hours and include fruit growers, who were previously exempt.

On the island of Terschelling, off the coast of Friesland, sheep have been banned from grazing and inspections of dykes have been stepped up amid concerns that the drought is causing cracks to appear.

World.title: Two women die trying to help a child in the sea at Callantsoog
World.content:
Two women died after going into the sea to help a child in trouble off Callantsoog in Noord-Holland on Tuesday afternoon.

A 39-year-old British woman, who had been missing overnight, was found dead on the beach at Groote Keeten, north of where the group ran into difficulty. A 26-year-old woman from Gelderland died on Tuesday after being pulled from the water and given CPR.

The two women went to the aid of a child who was at risk of drowning at about 4.30pm and then got into trouble themselves, broadcaster NOS reported. The child and another swimmer were brought ashore by the lifeguard service and taken to hospital for checks.

The alarm was raised at the Voordijk beach entrance, between Callantsoog and Groote Keeten. Four KNRM lifeboat stations took part in the search alongside the lifeguard service, the coastguard and police, using boats and helicopters from surrounding areas.

The search was called off shortly after 9pm on Tuesday because of the tide and resumed on Wednesday morning.

Police are not investigating the circumstances further, regional broadcaster NH reported. Neither woman has been named.

World.title: Belgium and Netherlands open new high-voltage power line
World.content:
The Netherlands and Belgium have opened a new high-voltage power line that will allow 30% more electricity to flow between the two countries.

The so-called Brabo III project connects Antwerp’s harbour to the Rilland high-voltage station across the border in Zeeland. The scheme is designed to reduce strain on the electricity grid and reduce electricity prices in both countries.

Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten and his Belgian counterpart Bart de Wever both attended the official opening in Antwerp. Jetten said the link was an important step towards ensuring European countries can produce their own energy.

“In recent years that has rapidly become a security issue,” he said. “It might not be how the Brabo III project started, but in today’s world it is an important element.”

De Wever said the line, which will supply power to companies such as BASF and Ineos, was “a new artery for our industry”.

Belgian grid operator Elia has spent 10 years building the power line, including two 192 metre-high masts at the Kallosluis, which links the Schelde to the Waaslandkanaal.

The Netherlands will be able to export up to 30% more solar and wind energy on high production days, while at other times it can import more power to meet rapidly increasing demand.

Utrecht has currently frozen all new applications for high-voltage electricity connections because the network has reached saturation point, while operator Tennet warned earlier in the year that some areas were approaching maximum capacity.

World.title: Bomb disposal experts called in at Limburg wildfire
World.content:
The wildfire near Venray in northern Limburg is under control, but efforts to fight the blaze are being hampered by the presence of unexploded munitions in the ground in an area that experienced heavy fighting at the end of the Second World War, the Limburg-Noord safety authority told broadcaster NOS.

Something that may be an unexploded shell was spotted in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve on Tuesday and experts from the defence ministry’s bomb disposal unit were called in. Heavy fighting took place around Venray during the war.

Explosions have been heard in the area over the past two days, but a fire service spokesman told NOS it is not certain these came from munitions. Intense heat can turn resin and moisture inside trees to steam, bursting the wood with a bang.

Keeping crews back from the buried ordnance is not slowing the operation down, the safety authority said, because the heat in those parts of the reserve would be unbearable either way.

Days of work ahead

“The fire stayed stable overnight,” Erik Thijssen of the safety authority told NOS on Wednesday morning. “There was no further spread.” He said the all-clear had not been given but the situation was “stable and manageable”.

Thijssen said putting the fire out completely would take several more days.

An emergency ordinance issued by the mayor of Venray on Tuesday afternoon remains in force. It bars people from entering the area and from flying drones over it.

Helicopters and crews

Defence ministry Chinook helicopters are due back in the air between 10am and 11am, the local safety authority told regional broadcaster L1 Nieuws.

The helicopters had dropped almost 900,000 litres of water on the fire by Tuesday evening, drawn from the Maas in buckets holding 7,600 litres.

Around 100 hectares have burned. The fire is being held inside “stop lines” – a railway line, an asphalt road and wide forest tracks – and firefighters are being rotated in from North Brabant, Utrecht, Drenthe and Friesland.

A fourth teenager has been arrested by police investigating a suspected terror plot, the Dutch prosecution service has said.

The 18-year-old was arrested at his home in Kesteren, Gelderland, on Friday evening by a police special intervention team (DSI) acting on information from the intelligence agency AIVD.

A magistrate in Rotterdam ordered him to be detained in custody for the next 14 days. His contact is restricted with his lawyer.

No weapons were found at his home and prosecutors said there were no signs an attack was imminent.

“At this point in the investigation we have not identified a clear target or moment for an attack,” the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie) said in a statement.

Last week three youths aged 16, 17 and 19 were arrested in overnight raids at homes in Rotterdam, Alkmaar and Eindhoven.

The eldest suspect, named as Mohammed K., was convicted two years ago of planning attacks on nightclubs and police stations in Belgium, none of which took place.

The other two were among a group of 14 people aged between 14 and 30 who were arrested last April on suspicion of inciting terrorism via the social media platform TikTok.

World.title: Dutch man arrested for racing on German motorway at 235km/h
World.content:
A Dutch man has been arrested for driving his Porsche 911 at speeds of up to 235 km/h on a German motorway while allegedly under the influence of cannabis.

The section of the A3 near Koblenz where he was stopped has no speed limit, but the 23-year-old man was pulled over for “extremely dangerous” driving after he weaved in and out of traffic and tailgated a police car.

A drug test revealed traces of THC, the active ingredient in cannabis, in his system. The man told police he ran a coffeeshop in Eindhoven with his father and regularly took the drug “for professional reasons”.

Police said traffic was relatively heavy for the time of day when the man was stopped just after midday on Monday. “It was only through good fortune that there were no traffic accidents,” they said.

The man has been charged with racing on the highway and dangerous driving. Police confiscated his driving licence and ordered him to pay €10,000 in bail before being released.

He was collected from the police station in Montabaur, 25km west of Koblenz, by his father.

In a separate incident across the border, a man from Rotterdam was arrested after reaching speeds of 246 km/h on the A15 while under the influence of drink and drugs.

The 40-year-old was stopped after passing a speed check near Papendrecht on Tuesday night on a section of motorway where the limit is 100 km/h.

His car was impounded and his licence seized by police after he was charged with dangerous driving and driving under the influence.

While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Russia condemns Poland’s “sacrilegious” demolition of Soviet monument
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the demolition of a Soviet-era monument in Poland, calling the decision “sacrilegious” and a “flagrant violation” of an agreement between the two countries on respecting places of remembrance. However, Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which financed the demolition, says that the monument was a “Soviet propaganda object” that was removed under a law requiring the “decommunisation” of public spaces. On Friday, around 150 residents in Pyrzyce, a town of 12,000 in northwestern Poland, gathered to watch the demolition of a monument to the Red Army that had stood there for decades. Initially, a memorial had been established in the town alongside a cemetery for Red Army soldiers in the immediate aftermath of World War Two, when the Soviets had driven the Nazi German occupiers out of Poland but then introduced a new communist government of their own. However, the soldiers’ remains were later moved to a military cemetery elsewhere in the region and the monument itself was redesigned and moved to another location within Pyrzyce. Its final form, created in 1984, was a huge rectangular concrete structure weighing several hundred tons and featuring a relief depicting the head of a Soviet soldier. A plaque said “Eternal glory to the fallen heroes 1941-1945” (a timeline that ignores the Soviet invasion and occupation of parts of Poland in 1939). Such Soviet monuments remained in many Polish towns and cities long after the fall of communism in 1989. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. However, only in 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, did the removal of Soviet-era monuments gather pace, with dozens demolished since then. Those efforts were led by the IPN, in particular during the time that the institute was headed by Karol Nawrocki between 2021 and last year, when he was elected president of Poland. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 At the start of this year, the local authorities in Pyrzyce began public consultations on removing their Soviet memorial, finding that a majority were in favour of the move, according to the IPN. In February, the town council voted to remove the monument. It will now be replaced with a new one commemorating Polish independence. “We are aware that this change evokes various, often very strong, emotions among residents,” wrote the local authorities on social media. “We respect both the voices of those supporting the actions taken and those who differ in their assessment of the current monument and its place in the history of Pyrzyce.” “We hope that independence – as a paramount value for all Poles – will unite residents beyond differences of opinion and assessment of the past. We want the emerging space to be a space of shared remembrance, reflection, and a dignified celebration of the most important national ceremonies.” The removal of the monument drew condemnation from the Russian embassy in Warsaw, which announced on Monday that it had lodged a formal protest. It called the decision the “latest sacrilegious step by the Polish authorities” and said that it “constitutes a direct and flagrant violation” of a 1994 agreement between Poland and Russia on respect for graves and other places of memory. “The illegal dismantling of monuments is an overt attempt to falsify history, to erase from the consciousness of the Polish nation the memory of the heroism of Soviet soldiers,” added the embassy. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 31 lipca 2026 r. w Pyrzycach (województwo zachodniopomorskie) na podstawie decyzji władz polskich został przeprowadzony demontaż pomnika ku czci poległych w latach 1941–1945 bohaterów – żołnierzy radzieckich. ❗️Ten kolejny świętokradczy krok… pic.twitter.com/cKhfFxIL9s — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) August 3, 2026 In response to such complaints from Russia, Poland has regularly pointed out that the 1994 agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. The IPN notes that such monuments were “Soviet propaganda objects”, designed to support the Moscow-backed communist regime, rather than genuine places of commemoration. Attending the demolition ceremony in Pyrzyce on Friday, IPN deputy president Karol Polejowski pointed out that the final version of the monument had been established in 1984 shortly after the period of martial law in Poland, when the authorities brutally clamped down on the democratic opposition. “Local communist activists, eager to curry favour with their Soviet masters, erected a monument honouring the Soviet army. This is not a symbol of liberation – it is a symbol of enslavement!” he declared, as the monument was torn down. 💪 Sowiecki obiekt propagandowy zostanie zastąpiony przez Pomnik Niepodległości, a przestrzeń wokół nowego monumentu stanie się godną sceną dla uroczystości patriotycznych. pic.twitter.com/5x4KEzG3Vb — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) July 31, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland’s WIG20 stock market index hits record high
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s blue-chip WIG20 stock market index hit its highest ever level on Monday, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year. According to market monitoring website MarketScreener, the index has gained just under 25% since the start of 2026, ahead of the Dutch AEX (16.9%) and Sweden’s OMX Stockholm (14.9%). The WIG20, which tracks the 20 largest and most liquid companies on the Warsaw Stock Exchange (GPW), climbed to 3,963.21 points on Monday, breaking its previous record of 3,940.53 points set in October 2007. It continues a rally that began in October 2022, since when the index has almost tripled in value. “The market continues to be supported by solid economic growth, rising consumer spending, and the prospect of further EU investment,” commented analysts from BNP Paribas, a bank, quoted by business daily Parkiet. “However, after such strong gains, we do not expect the pace of appreciation to remain as high as in recent years,” they added. On Monday, the biggest boosts to the WIG20 index were provided by PGE, Poland’s biggest power producer, and KGHM, a Polish multinational mining company, with their shares rising 3.3% and 1.6%, respectively. The surge was also supported by improving risk appetite across global markets following signs of a de-escalation in tensions in the Middle East. This has pushed WIG20 above the levels last seen 19 years ago, just before the index plunged almost 70% during the 2008 global financial crisis, and then suffered another sell-off during the euro zone debt crisis in 2011. Reform of one of the pillars of Poland’s pension system in 2014, which reduced the role of open pension funds, ushered in years of market stagnation and left the index struggling to meaningfully rebound in the following years. Another decline came during the COVID-19 pandemic and then in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In October 2022, however, the WIG20 started its rebound, rising by 195% since then. More than 30 Polish-listed companies have doubled in value over the past three years, including large-cap stocks such as Orlen, PKO BP, Bank Pekao, KGHM and Tauron, according to an analysis by economic journalist Rafał Hirsch published by news service WNP. Polish state energy firm Orlen has seen its market valuation rise to its highest ever level, and surpass Russia’s Gazprom for the first time https://t.co/w3po4izshJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 BNP Paribas’s analysts, however, note that, “despite a long-term upward trend and reaching record highs”, the Polish stock market “is still valued below many other European markets”. “Our stock market…remains significantly cheaper than the US market and most European markets, but at the same time, when viewed against its own historical performance, it is now relatively highly valued,” they said. Poland’s main stock index, the broader WIG, also closed on Monday at a record high of 148,428 points, having hit several records in recent months. Poland’s benchmark WIG stock index has passed the 100,000-point mark for the first time. Meanwhile, the Warsaw Stock Exchange has been the world’s best performing so far this year "It is a clear signal of the strength of our economy," says the PM's office https://t.co/fIgGWOLLn8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2025 Analysts warn, however, that unlike in the case of WIG, the WIG20’s record may prove short-lived because the benchmark is a price index, which excludes dividends. When companies in the index pay dividends, their share prices usually fall by about the same amount, which automatically pulls the index down even if nothing has changed in the companies themselves. Monday was the last day investors could buy shares in PKO BP and qualify for this year’s dividend. From Tuesday, the bank’s shares will trade ex-dividend, a move expected to reduce the WIG20 by about 0.8% because of PKO BP’s large weighting in the index. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that the group he leads, Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which is in the process of splitting from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, will soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes” over abortion or same-sex marriage. However, Morawiecki made clear he retains a hardline position on migration, saying he wants “zero Muslim migrants”, even legal ones, in Europe. He also categorically ruled out ever working with current Prime Minister Donald Tusk, but left the door open to potentially cooperating with the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is part of Tusk’s current ruling coalition, and with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), an opposition group. Morawiecki u Rymanowskiego: „Do 15 października założymy partię” No coraz ciekawiej 👀 pic.twitter.com/0FrMafvTEl — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) August 3, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki, a former PiS prime minister and current deputy leader of the party, in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 Most MPs in Development Plus, including Morawiecki himself, are still technically members of PiS, a situation that will only change if they decide to quit the party or if they are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks to complete. However, on Monday, in a lengthy interview with journalist Bogdan Rymanowski, Morawiecki confirmed that he would establish a new, separate party. That will happen “at the latest on 15 October”, when Development Plus is planning to hold a major convention, he added. Morawiecki claimed that a small group of hardliners, associated in particular with the nationalist Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska) party that was absorbed into PiS in 2024, were “devouring” PiS from the inside, pushing it in a more “radical” direction and seeking to take control of the party and its finances. The former prime minister argued that it had been a “colossal mistake” by PiS to try to compete with two rising far-right groups, Confederation and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), while abandoning the centre ground. He noted that this had coincided with the party’s support in polls falling to below 25%, its lowest level in 14 years and well below the 35% that the party won at the 2023 parliamentary elections, when Morawiecki was prime minister. Morawiecki also traced PiS’s problems back even further, pointing to the decision in 2020 to push for a near-total abortion ban. He claimed that he had, at the time, “warned [Kaczyński] repeatedly…that it would lead to disaster”. Subsequently, PiS fell from support of over 40% in polls to around 30% within a year. Morawiecki told Rymanowski that he and many of his colleagues in Development Plus support a return to the pre-2020 abortion law. “Poland doesn’t need the fervour of ideological disputes” over issues such as abortion and same-sex marriage, especially during a time of “crises, wars and disruptions”, said Morawiecki. “I want us to talk about strengthening the economy, strengthening security, restoring the job market, and how to prevent young people from thinking about leaving Poland again.” Poland’s prime minister has admitted it was a “mistake” for the ruling party to push for the constitutional court to introduce a near-total abortion ban in 2020. He claims “he has always been a supporter” of the abortion law that existed before the ruling https://t.co/QObza3Raxk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2023 The former prime minister also made clear that his overriding aim is “removing [Tusk] from power and overthrowing the Tuskist system”, which he characterised as a combination of “idleness” and “profound cynicism”, with the lack of any significant reforms disguised by “political marketing”. Asked if he would seek to achieve this by forming a coalition with the far-right Confederation, Morawiecki refused to rule it out, saying that “voters will decide” on the strength of various parties. “But I certainly won’t form any coalition with Tusk,” he clarified. However, Morawiecki suggested he would be willing to work with PSL and its leader, current deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, if they left the coalition with Tusk. PSL is the most conservative part of the current government. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 While Morawiecki generally laid out a vision of a relatively moderate centre-right party that he wants to create, he also made clear that he retains a hardline position on opposing Muslim immigration. “I would say zero Muslim immigrants at all. In Poland, absolutely zero…even into Europe,” he declared. Asked by Rymanowski to clarify if he was talking about only illegal migrants, or legal ones as well, Morawiecki said he was also referring to legal Muslim migrants. “We cannot accept them, because they will destroy our culture,” said Morawiecki. “After what I see Muslims doing in Europe, I don’t want to turn Europe into a Muslim caliphate….The French and Germans…are making a colossal mistake: destroying their own culture, destroying security, and destroying peace.” An Islamic group wants to establish a new prayer centre in Kraków for the growing local Muslim community The idea has drawn concern from some local residents and protests from right-wing groups, who say Poland should avoid "the mistakes of western Europe" https://t.co/ClCwusyhhp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Pole becomes first person to swim 160km Baltic Sea route between Sweden and Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
