World.title: Four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden, woman arrested
World.content:
London: A woman has been arrested after four people were stabbed in London’s Covent Garden, a bustling area in the centre of the capital that is full of attractions and popular with visitors.

The Metropolitan Police said early indications suggest it was a mental health-related incident and that scissors were recovered at the scene. Police said four men aged 34, 39, 42 and 52 were found with stab wounds and a 47-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault.

Police at the scene of the stabbings in Covent Garden. James Manning/PA via AP

The injured were taken to a trauma centre following the incident on Wednesday afternoon (London time) on Endell Street. Two were discharged and two remained with injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening.

“While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental health-related incident,” Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart said.

World.title: Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Michael Koziol August 6, 2026 — 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Democrats in the midwestern state of Michigan have chosen Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing Muslim health administrator, to be their candidate for the US Senate in a result with seismic consequences for the midterm elections and US politics. They rejected Haley Stevens, a four-term Democratic congresswoman heavily backed by the party establishment, despite outside groups spending more than $US60 million ($84.5 million) for her in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary ever. Progressive stars Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed in July. Bloomberg His victory comes at a time when Republicans led by US President Donald Trump are painting Democrats nationwide as being overtaken by communists who want to destroy America, end capitalism and adopt a range of policies that sit outside the mainstream. El-Sayed, who was backed by progressive hero Bernie Sanders and democratic socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, will be the Democratic candidate for a seat which the party must hold if they are to win control of the Senate in November.



The 41-year-old campaigned on a platform of taking private finance out of politics, putting money in the pockets of regular Michiganders, and universal healthcare. He promised higher taxes on the wealthy, and ending US military aid and arms sales to Israel. The contest was tighter than many recent polls predicted, with El-Sayed winning 48.5 per cent to 47.5, or about 15,000 votes. CNN and the Associated Press called the race for him just before 10am on Wednesday (midnight AEST), when 99 per cent of the counting was complete. Abdul El-Sayed at an election night party on Tuesday while the results were still too close to call. Bloomberg Both candidates called for unity. Stevens congratulated her opponent on winning a “thorough and rigorous campaign”, and pledged her support in the battle to come. Speaking in Detroit, El-Sayed said his campaign “took on a machine” and won. “What we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money,” he said. “My hope is that our democracy will never be the same.”



Michigan, a swing state that voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024, last sent a Republican to the US Senate in the 1990s. But Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, has brand recognition and only lost narrowly last time. Most experts say El-Sayed’s win makes it harder for Democrats to hold the seat, while strategists were soul-searching about the party’s direction, and whether it was moving too far to the left. The support of the Democratic establishment and a significant funding advantage was not enough to secure victory for Haley Stevens. Bloomberg Adrian Hemond, chief executive of Grassroots Midwest, a bipartisan Michigan-based public affairs group, told this masthead last week: “If he wins the primary and then loses the general election in the fall, it’s disastrous for national progressives.” El-Sayed is the first Muslim to win the Democratic nomination for the US Senate (though not the first Republican), and would be the first Muslim to enter the US Senate if he wins in November.



Unlike Ocasio-Cortez or Zohran Mamdani in New York, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. But he has attended their events in the past, and the DSA supported his campaign. “His policy platform is socialist,” Hemond said. El Sayed’s victory represents a heavy defeat for the Democratic elite. Stevens had endorsements from Michigan’s Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer, multiple senators and representatives, mayors and former officeholders. There were no results on Tuesday night with the race closer than most polls predicted. Bloomberg Sanders, appearing on CNN as the votes were still counted, said he couldn’t recall anything like it. “Abdul El-Sayed is taking on the entire Michigan Democratic establishment,” Sanders said. “He’s taking on the entire national Democratic establishment. He has been outspent 10 to one.”



Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake The $US60 million in outside funding supporting Stevens’ campaign included more than $US30 million from pro-Israel lobby groups, which became an important focus of the campaign. Polls show the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which funds pro-Israel candidates via super PACs, is a toxic entity among Democrats, especially younger ones - as is support for Israel more broadly. Stevens remained a staunch supporter of the Jewish state, and once told a Hanukkah event: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” El-Sayed ended up comfortably winning Kent County, which takes in the city of Grand Rapids. He also easily won the state capital, Lansing, and Ann Arbor, home to the University of Michigan.



Related Article Explainer

US election ‘A referendum on the president’: How do the midterms work? Stevens won Detroit, largely thanks to its majority population of African Americans, who are less likely to support left-wing candidates than white Democrats. Trump weighed in on Tuesday morning claiming, without evidence, that Wayne Country - which takes in Detroit - was one of the most corrupt voting areas in the US. “Great news for the Republican Party,” he said. “El-Sayed, a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner … Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs Shane Wright August 6, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Artificial intelligence could deliver the national economy a desperately needed productivity boost worth almost $120 billion and support the creation of tens of thousands of jobs, a nation-leading analysis has found. Compiled by consultancy EY, the modelling of AI’s impact on the ability of workers to boost output suggests the technology will increase the size of the economy by between 2.6 per cent and 3.2 per cent by the middle of the next decade. Data centres and the AI they support could deliver a much-needed boost to Australian productivity. Peter Rae That lift, worth between $95 billion and $116 billion, will contribute to an increase in jobs of between 36,000 and 44,000. The increase in productivity with AI is expected to generate an additional burst of business investment worth up to $38 billion. The country is in the midst of a data centre building boom, centred on NSW and Victoria, that by some comparisons will exceed the early 2010s mining boom that supercharged the economies of Western Australia and Queensland.



Related Article Exclusive

AI AI job disruption poised to upend Labor’s electoral map One Nation-style EY regional chief economist Cherelle Murphy said the research showed AI could turn around the nation’s poor productivity performance that many analysts believe has contributed to the sharp slowdown in Australians’ living standards and real wage growth. “The analysis shows that if AI-driven productivity gains flow through to investment, capacity and output, they could deliver a meaningful lift to economic growth,” she said. “The jobs story is not one of AI simply replacing workers across the economy. The modelling shows employment demand shifting towards sectors that benefit from stronger investment and household spending, while capital-intensive industries need fewer workers.” Critics of AI fear that in many cases the technology will wipe out jobs. There is limited evidence of that occurring in Australia to date.



Global human resources and payroll consultancy ADP on Wednesday released research suggesting only a quarter of all Australian workers believe their job is safe from elimination by AI, automation and changing demographics. But EY’s analysis shows many parts of the economy will need more staff because of AI. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy says not only will AI lift productivity, it will create more jobs. Alex Ellinghausen Of the expected increase in jobs, close to 10,000 are forecast to be in construction, with a similar number in retail and wholesale trade. Another 6000 are expected to be created in the transport, postal and warehousing sector. Financial services, hospitality, arts and recreation services, real estate and manufacturing are all tipped to enjoy an increase in jobs due to AI.



The research shows the construction sector is boosted because of the need to build data centres while installing equipment in those businesses that increase their use of AI-related technology. Oxford Economics estimates the value of data centre construction and fit-outs alone will climb from $1 billion in 2020 to $26 billion this year to $60 billion in 2030. Other sectors would enjoy a lift in jobs as the productivity gains delivered by the technology lifts real wages, which is expected to boost spending on goods and services. But both the agriculture and broad mining sectors are forecast to suffer job losses of almost 3000 each. These two sectors are capital-intensive, making them more susceptible to greater automation that would enable a reduction in workers and reduce cost overheads.



Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Murphy noted workforce mobility and “targeted reskilling” would be needed if businesses were to fully benefit from AI. “A key priority for employers and government should be helping workers move into the sectors and parts of businesses where demand is expected to grow,” she said. EY’s research, however, did find the surge in AI-related construction could add to inflation pressures across the economy as it had in the United States. But that would be offset by the deflationary impact of higher productivity once the technology was in place. It also found AI could lead to more rapid retail price changes.



”AI may also increase risks around price stability, giving businesses the ability to continuously monitor demand, input costs and competitor prices,” it found. “This could increase the frequency of price changes and the spread of price shocks.” Most economic and political focus has been on the tens of billions of dollars being spent on the construction of data centres. But EY noted there had also been a substantial increase in AI-related software, apps and cloud platforms, with growth running at 8.3 per cent over the past 12 months. Software investment had also contributed to a sharp 4.9 per cent annual lift in research and development, well above the 0.6 per cent annual average increase through the 2010s. World.title: ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandSchools ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity Catherine Strohfeldt August 5, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $55 million cash splash will boost enrolment capacity for primary schools in Brisbane’s west by up to 450 places and enable schools to ditch their demountables. However, the area’s high school was not so lucky. World.title: Four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden, woman arrested
World.content:
London: A woman has been arrested after four people were stabbed in London’s Covent Garden, a bustling area in the centre of the capital that is full of attractions and popular with visitors.

The Metropolitan Police said early indications suggest it was a mental health-related incident and that scissors were recovered at the scene. Police said four men aged 34, 39, 42 and 52 were found with stab wounds and a 47-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon and assault.

Police at the scene of the stabbings in Covent Garden. James Manning/PA via AP

The injured were taken to a trauma centre following the incident on Wednesday afternoon (London time) on Endell Street. Two were discharged and two remained with injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening.

“While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental health-related incident,” Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart said.

World.title: Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Michael Koziol August 6, 2026 — 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Democrats in the midwestern state of Michigan have chosen Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing Muslim health administrator, to be their candidate for the US Senate in a result with seismic consequences for the midterm elections and US politics. They rejected Haley Stevens, a four-term Democratic congresswoman heavily backed by the party establishment, despite outside groups spending more than $US60 million ($84.5 million) for her in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary ever. Progressive stars Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed in July. Bloomberg His victory comes at a time when Republicans led by US President Donald Trump are painting Democrats nationwide as being overtaken by communists who want to destroy America, end capitalism and adopt a range of policies that sit outside the mainstream. El-Sayed, who was backed by progressive hero Bernie Sanders and democratic socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, will be the Democratic candidate for a seat which the party must hold if they are to win control of the Senate in November.



The 41-year-old campaigned on a platform of taking private finance out of politics, putting money in the pockets of regular Michiganders, and universal healthcare. He promised higher taxes on the wealthy, and ending US military aid and arms sales to Israel. The contest was tighter than many recent polls predicted, with El-Sayed winning 48.5 per cent to 47.5, or about 15,000 votes. CNN and the Associated Press called the race for him just before 10am on Wednesday (midnight AEST), when 99 per cent of the counting was complete. Abdul El-Sayed at an election night party on Tuesday while the results were still too close to call. Bloomberg Both candidates called for unity. Stevens congratulated her opponent on winning a “thorough and rigorous campaign”, and pledged her support in the battle to come. Speaking in Detroit, El-Sayed said his campaign “took on a machine” and won. “What we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money,” he said. “My hope is that our democracy will never be the same.”



Michigan, a swing state that voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024, last sent a Republican to the US Senate in the 1990s. But Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, has brand recognition and only lost narrowly last time. Most experts say El-Sayed’s win makes it harder for Democrats to hold the seat, while strategists were soul-searching about the party’s direction, and whether it was moving too far to the left. The support of the Democratic establishment and a significant funding advantage was not enough to secure victory for Haley Stevens. Bloomberg Adrian Hemond, chief executive of Grassroots Midwest, a bipartisan Michigan-based public affairs group, told this masthead last week: “If he wins the primary and then loses the general election in the fall, it’s disastrous for national progressives.” El-Sayed is the first Muslim to win the Democratic nomination for the US Senate (though not the first Republican), and would be the first Muslim to enter the US Senate if he wins in November.



Unlike Ocasio-Cortez or Zohran Mamdani in New York, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. But he has attended their events in the past, and the DSA supported his campaign. “His policy platform is socialist,” Hemond said. El Sayed’s victory represents a heavy defeat for the Democratic elite. Stevens had endorsements from Michigan’s Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer, multiple senators and representatives, mayors and former officeholders. There were no results on Tuesday night with the race closer than most polls predicted. Bloomberg Sanders, appearing on CNN as the votes were still counted, said he couldn’t recall anything like it. “Abdul El-Sayed is taking on the entire Michigan Democratic establishment,” Sanders said. “He’s taking on the entire national Democratic establishment. He has been outspent 10 to one.”



Related Article US election Can a left-wing Muslim win the Midwest? Or are Democrats about to make a big mistake The $US60 million in outside funding supporting Stevens’ campaign included more than $US30 million from pro-Israel lobby groups, which became an important focus of the campaign. Polls show the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which funds pro-Israel candidates via super PACs, is a toxic entity among Democrats, especially younger ones - as is support for Israel more broadly. Stevens remained a staunch supporter of the Jewish state, and once told a Hanukkah event: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” El-Sayed ended up comfortably winning Kent County, which takes in the city of Grand Rapids. He also easily won the state capital, Lansing, and Ann Arbor, home to the University of Michigan.



Related Article Explainer

US election ‘A referendum on the president’: How do the midterms work? Stevens won Detroit, largely thanks to its majority population of African Americans, who are less likely to support left-wing candidates than white Democrats. Trump weighed in on Tuesday morning claiming, without evidence, that Wayne Country - which takes in Detroit - was one of the most corrupt voting areas in the US. “Great news for the Republican Party,” he said. “El-Sayed, a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner … Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAI Not just upheaval: AI could deliver $120b boost and more jobs Shane Wright August 6, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Artificial intelligence could deliver the national economy a desperately needed productivity boost worth almost $120 billion and support the creation of tens of thousands of jobs, a nation-leading analysis has found. Compiled by consultancy EY, the modelling of AI’s impact on the ability of workers to boost output suggests the technology will increase the size of the economy by between 2.6 per cent and 3.2 per cent by the middle of the next decade. Data centres and the AI they support could deliver a much-needed boost to Australian productivity. Peter Rae That lift, worth between $95 billion and $116 billion, will contribute to an increase in jobs of between 36,000 and 44,000. The increase in productivity with AI is expected to generate an additional burst of business investment worth up to $38 billion. The country is in the midst of a data centre building boom, centred on NSW and Victoria, that by some comparisons will exceed the early 2010s mining boom that supercharged the economies of Western Australia and Queensland.



Related Article Exclusive

AI AI job disruption poised to upend Labor’s electoral map One Nation-style EY regional chief economist Cherelle Murphy said the research showed AI could turn around the nation’s poor productivity performance that many analysts believe has contributed to the sharp slowdown in Australians’ living standards and real wage growth. “The analysis shows that if AI-driven productivity gains flow through to investment, capacity and output, they could deliver a meaningful lift to economic growth,” she said. “The jobs story is not one of AI simply replacing workers across the economy. The modelling shows employment demand shifting towards sectors that benefit from stronger investment and household spending, while capital-intensive industries need fewer workers.” Critics of AI fear that in many cases the technology will wipe out jobs. There is limited evidence of that occurring in Australia to date.



Global human resources and payroll consultancy ADP on Wednesday released research suggesting only a quarter of all Australian workers believe their job is safe from elimination by AI, automation and changing demographics. But EY’s analysis shows many parts of the economy will need more staff because of AI. EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy says not only will AI lift productivity, it will create more jobs. Alex Ellinghausen Of the expected increase in jobs, close to 10,000 are forecast to be in construction, with a similar number in retail and wholesale trade. Another 6000 are expected to be created in the transport, postal and warehousing sector. Financial services, hospitality, arts and recreation services, real estate and manufacturing are all tipped to enjoy an increase in jobs due to AI.



The research shows the construction sector is boosted because of the need to build data centres while installing equipment in those businesses that increase their use of AI-related technology. Oxford Economics estimates the value of data centre construction and fit-outs alone will climb from $1 billion in 2020 to $26 billion this year to $60 billion in 2030. Other sectors would enjoy a lift in jobs as the productivity gains delivered by the technology lifts real wages, which is expected to boost spending on goods and services. But both the agriculture and broad mining sectors are forecast to suffer job losses of almost 3000 each. These two sectors are capital-intensive, making them more susceptible to greater automation that would enable a reduction in workers and reduce cost overheads.



Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Murphy noted workforce mobility and “targeted reskilling” would be needed if businesses were to fully benefit from AI. “A key priority for employers and government should be helping workers move into the sectors and parts of businesses where demand is expected to grow,” she said. EY’s research, however, did find the surge in AI-related construction could add to inflation pressures across the economy as it had in the United States. But that would be offset by the deflationary impact of higher productivity once the technology was in place. It also found AI could lead to more rapid retail price changes.



”AI may also increase risks around price stability, giving businesses the ability to continuously monitor demand, input costs and competitor prices,” it found. “This could increase the frequency of price changes and the spread of price shocks.” Most economic and political focus has been on the tens of billions of dollars being spent on the construction of data centres. But EY noted there had also been a substantial increase in AI-related software, apps and cloud platforms, with growth running at 8.3 per cent over the past 12 months. Software investment had also contributed to a sharp 4.9 per cent annual lift in research and development, well above the 0.6 per cent annual average increase through the 2010s. World.title: The rise in One Nation popularity is scary
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters The rise in One Nation popularity is scary August 5, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. The rise of One Nation’s popularity in the polls is scary. One of the many reasons for the party’s popularity is the Labor Party and the Coalition have little on offer to encourage potential voters to look at them. One Nation has shown that it is a party that is against everything and has no real tangible and achievable policies. It is racist and anti-immigration, and people are falling for it. There are no policies on health, housing, defence, education and the many other platforms the major parties are promoting that Australians are concerned about. One Nation is a party based on fear, putting suggestions out there to scare the nation if they don’t get elected.

Alan Leitch, Austins Ferry, Tas Ignoring the party not the answer

Your correspondent proposes that The Age, ABC and The Guardian should retaliate against One Nation by ignoring it (Letters, 5/8). This wouldn’t work because a) it would make those media outlets look narrow-minded by not reporting the activities of a legitimate political party (and in the process reduce them to the same level of pettiness as One Nation), b) irresponsible, by not holding One Nation to account where necessary, and c) make them look like they were ganging up on One Nation, which would only support Pauline Hanson’s argument anyway. It would also be ineffective, because most One Nation voters are highly unlikely to read or follow any of those media organisations.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully The horror. The horror

The article ″⁣Victorian pick a self-described conspiracy theorist″⁣ (5/8) reminded me of The Age article by Michael Bachelard in which he wrote that the November election was shaping as ″⁣a classic pox-on-both-your-houses election″⁣, but if that pox were to kill off all our governing options, ″⁣what kind of zombies will be left holding power for the next four years″⁣. Bachelard said it was this prospect that caused him ″⁣to wake up in fright″⁣. Me too.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne



Another worldwide conspiracy at work

Like One Nation’s new Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, I, too, am a conspiracy theorist. However, my theory differs significantly from his. Given that all the right-wing populist parties throughout the world of which One Nation is one are all fiercely pro-fossil fuel, anti-renewable climate change deniers I would theorise that their policies are controlled by a cabal of the powerful global fossil-fuel industry.

Phil Alexander, Eltham No surprises in Pickering selection

Should we really be surprised Pauline Hanson has appointed a conspiracy theorist as One Nation’s leader in Victoria? In truth, Warren Pickering, like Malcolm Roberts, is the perfect candidate for those at the fringe. As with Donald Trump, Hanson pushes an anti-intellectual, anti-establishment rhetoric that demonises the media and the minorities and has boogeymen lurking behind every shadowy corner.

Matt Dunn, Leongatha Death knell or clarion call?

The selection of Warren Pickering should, for any thinking Victorian, sound the death knell of the party’s chances. He is a self-confessed conspiracy theorist. This could make recent One Nation converts nervous, but will suit the die-hards.

Greg Cooper, Mount Martha The importance of money in politics

Clinton Fernandes (Comment, 5/8) includes the quote from 19th century Republican businessman and senator Mark Hanna, ″⁣There are two things that are important in politics. The first is money, and I can’t remember what the second is.” This sounds like a policy statement from the Rinehart One Nation coalition.

Barry Doyle, Portarlington THE FORUM



Whither our suburbs?

The state government’s new discretionary height limits around so-called activity centres will result in sunless, soulless wind tunnels along our high street shopping strips, characterless concrete towers with no trees or permeable spaces, overlooking of existing dwellings, and additional parking and traffic management problems. What will happen to our previously high-scoring liveable city? Where is the community and council consultation and right of appeal against inappropriate developments that threaten to ruin our suburbs?

Vikki O’Neil, Ashburton Numeracy needs work

The NAPLAN reports (″⁣Victoria shines as national test scores falter″⁣, 5/8) show one very disturbing result. The results for numeracy from 2023-26 show those who “need additional support” or are “developing” are reasonably consistent across years 3, 5 and 7. There is also a consistent increase in underperformance from year 7 to year 9 in each year. For 2026, that increase for those needing support or developing is 23.9 per cent in year 7 to 29 per cent in year 9. Think about nearly a third of Victorian year 9s underperforming in mathematics. And what that means for their future and for Victoria.

There is clearly something going seriously wrong in the early years of secondary schooling. It is likely that a majority of year 7s are being taught mathematics by an out-of-field teacher. Teacher shortages may mean that the teacher also changes during the year. The resulting year 9 results are appalling. No wonder so many students are disengaged. Fixing the teacher problems may also be a good way to address youth crime.

Let’s begin by paying Victorian teachers properly and giving them working conditions that give them time to work with students who need extra help. Especially in year 7.

Jan Thomas, North Melbourne Difference a year makes

There is some useful information to be found in NAPLAN test results, but my biggest concern has always been between comparing one calendar year with the previous year, such as 2025 with 2026. The cohorts of students are different. For example, the year 5 students in 2025 do not sit a test in 2026. As a senior mathematics teacher for many years, I always accepted that one particular year 12 mathematics class may be gifted and highly competitive, whereas, the following year students may be less able.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Sun shines on Sunshine

Congratulations to Sunshine Primary School for its ongoing success in literacy and numeracy as shown in their NAPLAN results (″⁣Little ray of sunshine″⁣, 5/8). The whole school community must be proud. However, as indicated by the principal, this achievement is no fluke.

Victoria has been on an improvement path for many years utilising a strong evidence base (national and international) to inform teaching and learning. The focus has been on the quality of the teaching and learning in every classroom and leadership of and within schools. It has not been a quick fix, of phonics or any other ″⁣off the shelf″⁣ panacea as often reported in the media (although the teaching and learning of phonics has always been part of literacy learning). The challenge has been to stay the course and to reach and support every school and leader. We now know the impact and skill of the teacher is powerful and profound.

The work has involved enormous ongoing learning for all teachers, in professional development and collaboration and teamwork (whether they are new grads or old hands). And ongoing monitoring of students’ learning and development, using all manner of assessments and data collection.

Yes the job of teacher has changed to be an extremely demanding one, but after seeing these NAPLAN results in Victoria they should be very proud of their hard work paying off.

Julie Chandler, Blairgowrie No Marx for this

Any time you see the toddler-level accusation ″⁣communist″⁣ by a politician, in the words of the immortal John Clarke, “turn away and do the crossword”.

Greg Champion, Montmorency



Old tropes die hard

Both sides of our family hailed from the Eolian Islands, north of Sicily. They arrived in Melbourne more than 100 years ago. I presumed our DNA would have identified us as “Italian”.

In fact, it identified us as Greek, Sardinian, Iberian, Sephardic Jew, West Asian, Ashkenazi Jewish, but zero per cent Italian!

So much for the monoculture. We are all boat people.

During WWII, our family’s “odyssey”, despite having lived and worked here for multiple decades, included racial abuse, disruption of the family fruit business by violent thugs, intimidation by authorities and accusations of stealing jobs from “real Australians”.

This was par for the course in those days.

But old tropes die hard. Opponents of cultural and religious diversity are now renewed and morphing into potential future political leaders.

To look forward however we must look back, to learn from past lessons of fear, xenophobia and questionable conspiracies.

Peter Russo, West Brunswick Climate strategy

Some would have us believe that, when the sun doesn’t shine and the wind doesn’t blow, we can’t rely on renewable energy so we need nuclear power as a back-up.

However, as the heatwave in Europe is showing, nuclear generation requires a lot of water for cooling and when that’s in short supply, generation must be scaled back as is happening now.

Logically, therefore, we need a more strategic approach like reducing the catastrophic warming of the planet before all options are exhausted.

Perhaps the answer is to burn more coal and gas to supply the energy we need. But wait, that’s how we got in this situation in the first place.

John Annison, Lilydale Come to Surrey Hills

Repurposing and developing the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys in Surrey Hills should be welcome news (″⁣Anger over push to turn one of nation’s oldest orphanages into apartments″⁣, 4/8).

This site of our significant history has been sadly vacant for a very long time. Let’s welcome more people into Surrey Hills, which is so well-endowed with all types of public transport, shops, schools and parks. We may not be in an ″⁣activity centre area″⁣ as such, but there is an abundance of services here for more people to share.

Jane Hudson, Surrey Hills Torpedo sub-portfolios

Although Premier Ben Carroll has acted commendably to reduce his new ministry down to 20, there remains a need for rationalisation of the excessive 63 different sub-portfolios now crammed into those 20 ministries.

Some arrangements are sound – for example, the combination of energy and resources, environment and climate action in one portfolio makes sense as these are related areas.

However, that contrasts with the jumbled portfolio arrangements for jobs, industry and advanced manufacturing, and trade, tourism and investment, which are split between two portfolios, yet are just different outcomes of or areas needing action as elements of economic development, which itself is shown in a third portfolio, when maybe two portfolios would have sufficed.

And why is prevention of family violence not included in the portfolio with police and crime prevention, and why is community sport split off from sport?

Thomas Hogg, East Melbourne Potholes everywhere ...

Please can people stop banging on about potholes.

Having just returned from a road trip that took us through Victoria and parts of NSW and Queensland, it is apparent that these states all have issues with the ubiquitous pothole.

We even saw a sign in NSW that read “potholes trialling” – we weren’t sure if they were trialling new shapes for potholes or working on a method of successfully repairing the wretched things.

Some suggested causes of potholes range from heavy trucks to extreme weather conditions. There have certainly been plenty of the latter in recent times.

After working on our own remedy, we have decided there is a very simple solution for this ongoing problem – bring back the Country Roads Board.

Graham and Louise Bell, Blackburn



... Even in Brisbane

Victoria’s Liberal promises to fix potholes could be treated with scepticism. Brisbane has had 20 years of Liberal government. Yet in inner Brisbane some potholes seem to reach to the centre of the Earth.

Glenn Wood, Bardon, Qld An election possibility

Why has no one been honest about the possibility of a hung parliament after the November state election? I was living in Tasmania in 1989 when the ALP and the Tasmanian Greens had to form a government because that is what the voting public determined in their voting at the election.

The reality is that if Pauline Hanson’s party gains the relevant numbers then they will have to govern with one of the major parties. That is our democracy at work. That is why voters need to understand this possibility when they vote on November 28.

Maree Williams, Kew In whose interests?

I agree with your correspondent (Letters, 5/8). Just because someone is super wealthy does not mean they have the best interests of the community at heart. In fact, they often get rich by self-interest. Not the best quality for politics.

Kim Abrahams, Fairhaven



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Should One Nation be known as One News?

George Reed, Wheelers Hill There are conspiracy theorists galore for One Nation party opponents to explore. Warren Pickering is one such person.

Eric Palm, Gympie, Qld The contrast between the One Nation candidates and what they believe in and the exemplary work of independent senator David Pocock, in regard to wagering and taxation, is extraordinary.

Peter Baddeley, Portland



If Pauline Hanson is moderately successful at the Victorian and next federal election, all the major parties have only themselves to blame.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Furthermore

New Zealand has shown us the way on greyhound racing. How long will it be before the industry is shut down in Australia?

John Walsh, Watsonia Gambling advertising in any form should be banned, and we need a powerful federal industry regulator. Full stop.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn With children struggling with the basics of learning, let’s help them by stopping confusing fads like using “learning” as a noun.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Re potholes, the only way to fix the problem is to run annual Tour de Victoria bicycle races.

Keith Robinson, Glen Waverley



If all Jetstar passengers paid for overhead luggage storage there would be no improvement in boarding and in punctual departures.

Virginia Heller, St Kilda Not sure the world could cope if Donald Trump won the mid-terms as Clinton Fernandes (Comment, 5/8) suggests.

Marie Nash, Balwyn Finally

It is the little things in life that matter. Every morning, rain or shine, a kindly neighbour picks up our delivered newspapers and puts them on top of our letter box.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East

World.title: Commerce Commission takes Foodstuffs South Island to court
World.content:
The Commerce Commission says it is taking Foodstuffs South Island to court, alleging "far-reaching anti-competitive conduct that deprived customers of cheaper prices".

The competition watchdog alleged it implemented and enforced a widespread restriction on independently owned Pak'nSave stores discounting selected products.

Foodstuffs South Island is a co-operative, and the owner of New World, Pak'nSave and Four Square in the south.

Under the franchise model, individual South Island Pak'nSave supermarkets are supposed to be able to compete on pricing, discounts and promotions, Commerce Commission chair John Small said.

"Instead, we allege FSSI (Foodstuffs South Island) applied guidelines and rules that stopped these independently owned and operated supermarkets from offering certain discounts unless they received prior approval," he said.

The commission believed the conduct constituted resale price maintenance, which was prohibited under the Commerce Act.

It said Foodstuffs South Island centrally set a "super deal" promotion price for a product, and did not allow franchisees from discounting below the price, unless Pak'nSave obtained prior approval.

The commission said franchisees were also not allowed to discount any other product in the same category below the "super deal" promotional price.

The accusations also included that Foodstuffs South Island set an "every day low price" centrally, primarily for shelf staple goods, and did not allow Pak'nSaves from applying further discounts on these products without prior approval.

"We will argue the alleged anti-competitive conduct was widespread, with FSSI's guidelines covering all South Island Pak'nSave franchisees for a period of at least several years," Small said.

World.title: Tiaki Wai apologises after Wellington residents fight bills for water they can't use
World.content:
Wellington residents forced out of their homes due to storm damage have been landed with bills from Tiaki Wai - despite not using any water.

Late on Wednesday Tiaki Wai apologised for the bills, saying they were a mistake as it gets to grips with running the new water entity.

Tiaki Wai has been sending its first bills to residents over the past couple of weeks.

Aaron Pahl fled his Stokes Valley house in February, as the base of his home slid down the hill in a fierce storm.

That left his family home hanging exposed - and he was told by the council he couldn't return.

"Nah, nah, we're not allowed to live in it, there's a sign on the door saying if we live in it we get a $200,000 fine for every day we reside in it."

Currently dealing with claims with the Natural Hazard Commission - and facing huge costs to fix his home - Pahl said a $562 bill due on 1 September added insult to injury.

The view from Aaron Pahl's house after a slip left the house uninhabitable. Supplied

He said he should not have to pay for water he couldn't use.

"Surely they could have communicated amongst themselves and said, 'alright, let's not send it to this bunch'.

"But they sent it anyways and I'm like, 'Well, you guys can fly a kite I'm not paying it', you know. I've got enough to deal with at the moment let alone paying a bloody water bill for something I can't even use."

Hutt City Council has granted him a rates remission, and he said the same should apply to his water bill.

"The council have said I'm not allowed to live in my house, right? So I'm not going to be using water, my sewage isn't going to be working, like I'm not going to have any toilets flushing or anything like that, so I don't feel like I have to pay it for that."

Wellington City Council said three buildings were issued with dangerous building notices following April's flash flooding and 104 properties qualified for rates remission.

Hutt City Council said six buildings were white and yellow-stickered following April's storms, but could not provide the numbers of properties qualifying for rates remission.

Berhampore resident Josh Palmer and his wife scaled a two-metre fence with their baby when floods ripped through their home in April.

The home was unliveable, he said and had been deemed a "total loss".

Palmer said the family had been living elsewhere ever since and had been granted rates remission by the Wellington City Council.

But it was different story for the nearly $500 Tiaki Wai water bill.

"It wasn't a shock that we got the bill as we did know that that was going to happen. But we applied to ... not have to pay that bill, which got rejected.

"So that was the big shock to us."

Flooding in April 2026 caused significant damage to Josh and Ali Palmer's newly-renovated home in Berhampore, Wellington. Supplied / Josh and Ali Palmer

Palmer said the family was appealing that decision, and hoped Tiaki Wai would "see a bit of reason", but said the whole situation was "pretty annoying".

"Having to chase this up is just more work for us on top of all the insurance and everything we have to do with the fact that we've lost our house.

"It just adds to our plate."

'I apologise' - Tiaki Wai says teething issues due to 'massive change'

Tiaki Wai's chief executive Michael Brewster said he was sorry the bills were sent by mistake as staff got to grips with running the new entity.

He said those getting rates rebates for storm-damaged properties would either get lower water bills, or none at all - depending on how the council was doing its rates remission policy for the property.

Brewster urged anyone in a similar situation with a flood-damaged home to get in contact.

"It's pretty clear we missed this piece, and didn't get it right, and so to them I do apologise. However, we are dealing with four different councils, four different billing systems, a massive change - so some things are going to be missed, that's not an excuse, just a reality."

Tiaki Wai's chief executive Michael Brewster. RNZ

Some residents said they've been shocked by the bills, and confused about how to pay - with Lower Hutt residents initially unable to set up regular bill payments for their annual bill on the Payble App, to spread the costs.

Brewster said that issue had now been corrected.

He said if people were unable to pay their bills, they should contact Tiaki Wai.

"There's a cost of living crisis...if you are struggling to pay my message is please contact us, we do have hardship policies to contact customers - who are genuinely struggling."

However he said people simply refusing to pay their bills without contacting Tiaki Wai, was a different situation.

That could mean debt collection.

World.title: How does your pay compare to the average?
World.content:
Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

If you've felt like it's getting harder to keep up with the cost of everything, you're not wrong.

Data released on Wednesday by Stats NZ shows that most New Zealanders aren't getting pay increases that keep up with the rate of inflation.

Across all sectors, labour cost index data showed salary and wage rates were up 2 percent over the year to June, and 0.6 percent compared to the previous quarter.

The average ordinary time hourly earning is now $44.62, according to the Quarterly Economic Survey.

Average weekly earnings including overtime for full-time equivalent employees increased to $1730.

The private sector was up 2 percent annually and the public sector 1.7 percent.

Across the industries, wood and paper products manufacturing had the largest annual increase up 3 percent, followed by mining, local government administration, arts and recreation services and the group Stats NZ refers to as "other services" all up 2.5 percent.

Transport postal and warehousing, financial and insurance services and administrative and support services were up 2.3 percent.

Retail trade and accommodation had a 1.8 percent increase, construction wages were up 1.6 percent and electricity, gas, water and waste services were up 1.2 percent.

Kiwibank economist Alexandra Turcu. Supplied / Kiwibank

Kiwibank economist Alexandra Turcu said wages were going backwards compared to an annual inflation rate of 4.1 percent. "The cost of things has increased twice as much as the wages that the average Kiwi is getting."

She said inflation had started outpacing wage growth just after Covid hit New Zealand. "We really haven't had a reversal stick around for very long. We had a few quarters in about 2024 where wages started to outpace inflation for a little bit but it didn't last. It's really been weighing on Kiwi consumers for a long time."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub agreed. He said while average take-home weekly pay was going up it was often because people were working more hours. "If you've had the same job over the last year then your real income has fallen by 2 percent."

He said data such as the ANZ consumer confidence survey showed people had been feeling "persistently negative" about their finances for the last few years. "I think that's what we're seeing, that sustained feeling of being under pressure because people's purchasing power has been eroded. So much of the inflation has been about necessities, which really erodes people's purchasing power."

ANZ senior economist Matthew Galt said using the Quarterly Employment Survey, average hourly earnings were up 2.8 percent over the year. This measures what employees receive, including the effect of things like promotions or additional hours, while the labour cost index measures the cost of a unit of labour for an employer.

He said, by this measure, wages had increased faster than inflation on average since 2020 but by less than was typical before the pandemic. "Real wages have risen by an average of 0.8 percent per year since 2020 compared with 1.1 percent in the two decades before 2020.

"There have been two periods in recent years where inflation has outpaced wage growth: first in 2021 and 2022 when inflation surged, and again over the past year as higher fuel prices have pushed inflation higher. Periods of high inflation since 2021 - including for many necessities, together with a softer labour market, are likely contributing to the sense of ongoing cost-of-living pressures."

Turcu said inflation was being pushed up by the conflict in the MIddle East. "Once that's resolved we're likely to see those cost pressures come off and prices come back down or at least not increase as quickly any more. That can give time for wages to catch up."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. Supplied

Eaqub said things would only improve when the labour market was sufficiently strong that the bargaining power for wages moved from employers to employees. "We're not there yet. There is a huge pool of people who are currently unemployed and there is very few vacancies. It's still Hunger Games, in terms of looking for jobs. And when you're desperately looking for a job it's very hard to secure big increases in pay. Also because the businesses don't have the money to pay. It's not like profitability is booming."

Stats NZ said 46 percent of pay increase in the year to June were attributed to the cost of living, compared to 41 percent last June.

Only 21 percent were because employers were matching market rates and 13 percent were because they needed to retain staff.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said that was probably something that would alarm the Reserve Bank. "It suggests that people's inflation expectations have increased to the extent to which they're going to their employer and saying 'well I need a cost-of-living adjustment' and that is the mechanism by which second-round type impacts on inflation occur."

World.title: Mental distress among new parents carries long-term social cost of $2b a year - report
World.content:
A new report estimates the cost of mental distress among new parents carries a long-term social cost of more than $2 billion a year.

Clinical mental distress includes perinatal OCD, birth trauma and PTSD, postpartum psychosis, as well as the more commonly known postpartum depression, which affects about 15 percent of the population.

But the cost estimate rose to $4.3b when it considered sub-clinical distress, too - things like sadness, anxiety and trouble sleeping.

The report was commissioned by the Tindall Foundation, a private family philanthropic foundation, and written by Auckland-based consultancy Social Prism using data from sources including the Ministry of Health, Te Whatu Ora, and Stats NZ.

It found up to half of māmā and birthing parents - around 29,000 people annually - experienced mental distress during pregnancy and the early years.

Many of the costs of mental distress soon after childbirth were felt later through health, education, welfare, child protection and justice systems.

Ashlee McCormick, the foundation's donations programme manager, said the estimate was conservative, and likely an under-estimate.

"Probably the scale of distress is much bigger," she said. "Around half of birthing parents experience some level of distress, so it's about 29,000 women every year."

There was a gap in community care, she said, which could be improved with more funding and better national policies.

"When mums are well, they're better able to care for their babies, recognise their cues, it helps build a better bond between mum and baby," she explained.

"And that we know if that bond is strong and there's a trusted adult or caregiver figure, it helps with the social cognitive development of those babies, which helps you be more school ready, which leads to better educational outcomes."

It also reduced the chance children would grow into adults who interacted with the justice system, which could be "a hugely expensive exercise", she said.

Eli Maiava founded the NGO Whare Manaaki o Te Tai Poutini in Greymouth in 2020, and she's also tangata whenua co-lead of the support service Te Hokinga Mai, funded by the Tindall Foundation - both focused on supporting whānau wellbeing in the community.

She said community was often the first place families reached out to - and it would be more effective to invest in early support, than to pay the cost in the justice and health systems later on.

"Those first 2000 days are integral for brain development, and that leads us into education, into mental health, into decisions that we make as adults," she said.

"Working in these spaces and seeing the challenges that whānau face, it really frustrates me that all of the investment is at the other end, when all of the impact of not being supported in those early days comes to bear."

World.title: 'There are no jobs': Support services warn unemployment crisis driving rising violence
World.content:
Support services in the Far North are warning that rising unemployment is pushing more families into extreme hardship, as the region grapples with the country's highest jobless rate.

The latest statistics suggested that unemployment had risen to its highest rate in more than a decade.

Northland had overtaken Auckland as the region recording the highest unemployment at 8.8 percent, up from 5.1 percent.

Those working on the frontline said rising joblessness was leading to growing demand for food assistance, worsening mental health and increasing family violence.

Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services chief executive Moana Eruera said her organisation had seen a significant increase in families seeking help for unemployment combined with rising living costs.

The organisation's social supermarket, Whata Kai, received 181 referrals in July alone as more families sought help with food, rent, power bills and other essentials.

Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services chief executive Moana Eruera. Supplied / Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services

Eruera said the Far North's rural geography compounded financial pressures, with many residents travelling long distances to access supermarkets, health services and other necessities.

She said financial hardship often had wider social consequences.

"When there's that kind of financial stress on families, you often see an increase in the factors that contribute to family harm."

The organisation's family violence teams were already under significant pressure.

"They are very busy supporting whānau."

Eruera said demand for food support continued to grow despite funding becoming harder to secure.

While the social supermarket operates in partnership with Foodstuffs, she said it receives no direct government funding and relied on the organisation's own investment alongside philanthropic support.

"The demand is growing, and we hope we can sustain the level of service we're able to provide."

Packed bags of food. Supplied / Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services

'There are no jobs'

The director of community advocacy organisation Nga Taonga o Kaikohe, Megan Hepi, estimated between 7500 and 8000 people across Northland were currently looking for work, while only about 600 to 700 vacancies were available across the region.

She said the situation was expected to worsen following the closure of the Juken timber mill near Kaitaia, with dozens of workers expected to lose their jobs.

"Those are the entry-level jobs our rangatahi can get into."

She said young people were being hit particularly hard, with many leaving the region in search of work.

"Even my own son was ready to work. His employer had to shut down because they couldn't afford the rising costs, and he's now moved to Auckland to find full-time employment."

Nga Taonga o Kaikohe director Megan Hepi. Nick Monro

Hepi said many people receiving support wanted to work but simply could not find employment.

"You can't train your way out of unemployment when there are more people looking for work than there are jobs," she said.

"If every unemployed person went into study tomorrow and graduated, there still wouldn't be enough jobs for them."

She said increasing pressure on people already struggling financially was taking a toll on their wellbeing.

"People are struggling. They're depressed. We're seeing more mental health issues because of the financial pressure."

Hepi said Northland needed more jobs rather than more training programmes.

"We have people here with a lot of skill, but when there are only a handful of businesses employing people ... Everyone can't work at New World."

She believed solutions needed to come from within the region, including creating more small businesses and relocating some government jobs north.

World.title: Commerce Commission needs more firepower to boost competition and wages - economist
World.content:
An economist says political parties should look to give the Commerce Commission more firepower in an effort to boost competition and wages.

It comes as unemployment hits an 11-year high, with around 171,000 New Zealanders out of work, and as Labour edged ahead again as the party most trusted to manage the economy according to the latest Ipsos Issues Monitor.

Bagrie Economics' lead economist Cameron Bagrie told RNZ he didn't see any political party attempting to address the cost of living and low wages by creating more competition.

He said the unemployment figures confirmed that the economy took a "detour" in the second quarter.

"We got the stuffing knocked out of us in the second quarter because of higher fuel prices" and the "numbers weren't flash", he said.

He suggested competition policy was what was needed to fix both the cost of living crisis and the income crisis.

"Wages are low in New Zealand compared to overseas counterparts."

He explained that if there's more competition across sectors, that drives down costs, and more competition across industries, that drives innovation and productivity growth.

"That's where you're addressing both crises.

"I don't see an awful lot of political parties out there at the moment connecting the two.

"Competition policy in New Zealand is too light touch."

Bagrie says the economy is going through a significant transition, away from a model of immigration, tourism, and "selling more expensive houses to each other". RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Bagrie thought the Commerce Commission needed "some guns" by making it independent, giving it a charter and a remit to "go really hard" in driving greater competitive settings.

He suggested giving it a target of making inflation between 1 to 3 percent and giving it "full operational independence to go about that".

He did think the economy was at a turning point though, a point that was hit about six months ago.

"The weight of economic evidence is pretty clearly showing that the economy is moving forward," he said, but that wouldn't be showing in the second quarter of data the latest figures refer to.

Currently, he said unemployment was up, inflation was up and interest rates were moving up, so "economically, that's not what you call a great trifecta of any government that's looking to get re-elected".

But he acknowledged the economy was going through a significant transition, away from a model of immigration, tourism, and "selling more expensive houses to each other".

It was now built around business investment, productivity growth and natural resources, and just "doing things a little bit differently".

"That economic transition does not happen overnight."

He acknowledged things take time to deliver, "You've got to get infrastructure right. You've got to get the education system right. You've got to get research and development right."

He also mentioned getting the banking system right, "because there's no point pumping money continually into the housing market".

World.title: City Rail Link opening date revealed as 13 September
World.content:
Thirty-nine days.

The opening date for Auckland's City Rail Link has been revealed as Sunday, 13 September, 39 days away.

An Auckland Transport billboard on Fanshawe Street seen early Thursday morning announced the date.

The $5.5 billion CRL is New Zealand's largest transportation infrastructure project, and construction has been going on for the past 10 years.

Until now, its opening date had been kept tighting under wraps, with Auckland councillor Richard Hills earlier saying people were getting frustrated.

"Is there any way in the next couple of days that it can be announced what month? Because there are a lot of people getting upset, concerned. There's a lot of businesses who just want hope."

CRL open days

Auckland Transport, City Rail Link Limited and KiwiRail will be opening the new stations to the public through a series of 'First Look' events. These will be free, ticketed sessions, but numbers will be limited.

They will be held over consecutive Saturdays in August: 8 August - First Look at Maungawhau, 15 August - First Look at Karanga-a-Hape, 22 August - First Look at Te Waihorotiu.

The free tickets for these will be available one week ahead of each event.

At peak, trains will run every five minutes through the city centre and on average around 10 minutes elsewhere on the network. At off-peak the new lines will operate every 15 minutes throughout the day, including weekends, compared with every 20 minutes at present.

World.title: Another frosty start as MetService warns of negative temperatures
World.content:
Many places in the country will be waking up to freezing weather on Thursday, with MetService warning of double-digit negative temperatures in parts of the south.

MetService says Auckland has had its coldest temperatures recorded this year overnight.

Whenuapai Airport recorded -1.7 degrees on Thursday, and Auckland Airport was 1.5degC before 5am.

Metereologist Luis Fernandes said Auckland could be set for even lower temperatures on Thursday evening.

Invercargill has also reached its coldest this year, at -5.3 degrees early this morning.

Other parts of the North Island that saw sub-zero temperatures overnight, including Taumarunui, Taupo and Hamilton.

In the South Island, Christchurch, Queenstown and Alexandra all recorded temperatures below -3 degrees.

Transpower says there could be another record demand for electricity as cold weather grips the country.

Mount Cook Village was forecast to drop to -10°C on Thursday morning.

MetService meteorologist Katie Lyons said widespread frosts were forecast.

"We've got a big ridge of high pressure which is giving a lot of clear skies, and that means cold temperatures, good cooling so people will be waking up to lots of frosts around the country," she said.

"Places like Auckland could be anywhere between -2°C all the way up to 4°C. The likes of Wellington it could be anywhere between 0°C and 4°C."

Transpower said there could be another record demand for electricity on Thursday, after the country's highest ever electricity use was recorded on Wednesday morning.

The power grid operator issued a notice to power companies advising there would be a potential shortfall of energy at peak times over the next couple of days.

Warnings were in place on Thursday and Friday between 7.30am and 8.30am.

Lyons said the cold snap was expected to end by the weekend.

"For most places into Friday that cold will continue," she said.

"The West Coast of the South Island will be the first to slowly see those temperatures rise into Friday, and then for the rest of the country on Saturday it will feel like more of a return to normal as we get the next frontal feature moving in from the Tasman with some northwesterly winds."

'We're absolutely ecstatic' - skifield boss

Whakapapa ski-field. Supplied/ Ruapehu Alpine Lifts

Whakapapa general manager of operations Steve "Youngman" Manunui said it was -7degrees Celsius at the ski-field's base area on Thursday - ideal conditions for snowmaking.

Whakapapa GM discusses Mt Ruapehu ski season Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The lingering impact of Covid-19 and financial pressures had made this a make-or-break season for Whakapapa and Turoa, he said.

It was under new ownership and was seeing the best start to the season since before the pandemic.

"We're absolutely ecstatic with the start to the winter, best start since pre-Covid actually."

The El Nino phase was delivering cooler, drier temperatures, he said.

The cycle of storms over the last three weeks had been welcome and in between there had been some fine sunny spells that had drawn large numbers of customers.

Manunui said the skifields were in an ideal location in the middle of the North Island, so they were able to attract customers from all over the North Island.

"The good thing is these weather patterns look like they're going to continue for a wee while ... we're setting ourselves up nicely for spring and traditionally we go right through to Labour weekend.

World.title: 'Gone down like a lead balloon': Ex-FA boss on FIFA's World Cup backflip
World.content:
"It's gone down like a lead balloon."

This is David Gallop's view of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-infamous World Cup privatisation proposal.

"It's so far off passing the pub test that I think it's like he let off a stink bomb in the middle of the pub and people ran screaming, leaving half a schooner behind," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"That's how poorly it's been received."

Mr Gallop has been one of Australia's foremost sport's administrators. He was CEO of the NRL from 2002-2012 before jumping ship to become the boss of Football Federation Australia for seven years until his tenure ended in 2019.

He has watched on this past week as Mr Infantino's failed sell-off plan has evolved into a full-blown crisis over his leadership.

"He's definitely under pressure now … to throw out an idea like this that's gone down so badly," he said.

Mr Infantino's proposal, dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have seen the commercial rights of FIFA's most popular tournaments, including the World Cup, transferred to a private company, and a 20 per cent stake sold to investors, valued at $20 billion.

It's been reported Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, was one of the private equity figures behind the plan.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump was under scrutiny at the World Cup. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

"Anytime you sell anything, you need to have good, compelling reasons, but particularly so when it comes to something like the World Cup and ... sport in general," Mr Gallop told 7.30.

"You've got to know that you really need to do it. You really need the money. What are you getting for the slice of the asset and what are you giving up?

"Clearly people have not liked the idea that private investment, and therefore, a profit motive that comes away from the game to those private investors would be something that FIFA would contemplate."

'One-off sugar hit'

Mr Gallop said privatisation was not inherently wrong but required an overwhelming strategic and financial case to be valid.

"It will be a mistake to burn the furniture to heat the house," he said.

"You need to be setting up your sport and the business of your sport for sustainability, not for a one-off sugar hit of capital.

"These are the questions that have to be answered when one is looking at private sale of these effectively community assets that people feel strongly about."

FIFA President Gianni Infantino's plan to privatise has been met with derision by many football bodies. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

The proposal offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each, but Mr Gallop said FIFA's financial position only heightened questions about why such a proposal had been pursued.

"FIFA has $5 billion in cash now after the World Cup," he said.

" I think that's one of the reasons why a proposal to sell an equity stake has fallen so flat. They're not desperate for money. "

Within three days of the proposal, Mr Infantino and FIFA scrapped the plans.

Europe's UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and Asia's AFC, which Australia is member of, all opposed the plan.

UEFA, CONCACAF, as well as a growing number of national federations have taken it further by withdrawing their support of Mr Infantino's leadership.

Football Australia's chair Anter Isaac and CEO Martin Kugeler both declined an interview with 7.30.

The organisation has welcomed the decision by FIFA to scrap the privatisation proposal but is yet to weigh-in on Mr Infantino's, now under siege, leadership.

Mr Gallop said Australia's influence on the world game came less through political power than integrity.

Infantino's 'blotted copybook'

The integrity of Mr Infantino, like that of his predecessor Sepp Blatter has now been called into question.

Former FIFA President Sepp Blatter's tenure ended due to corruption. (Reuters: Stefan Wermuth)

Mr Infantino was elected in 2016 promising to restore confidence in FIFA, following a number of corruption scandals that occurred under Mr Blatter's 17-year reign as president.

Mr Gallop's time at FA straddled the terms of both men. He was also CEO in 2010, when Australia's bid to host the 2022 World Cup was beaten by Qatar, a decision that was mired in controversy and allegations of corruption.

"There was a bit of a stench around FIFA and Gianni came in with a pitch of transparency, accountability, consultation and putting football first," Mr Gallop said.

" I think it's fair to say this proposal, albeit backflipped on, has blotted his copybook in respect to what people expected from him and from his presidency. "

"[Especially} coming hot off the heels of a number of other contentious decisions, including the lifting of the red card on the USA player during the tournament."

United States' Folarin Balogun's red card was rescinded during the World Cup after a call from Trump to Infantino. (AP: Jeff Chiu)

Despite calls for Mr Infantino's resignation growing louder, Mr Gallop said his tenure at the top of world football might not be over just yet.

"I don't think it's necessarily so that he won't get re-elected. He has some big confederations against him at the moment, but he has others where FIFA has carefully funded development in a lot of smaller nations," he said.

Mr Gallop remembers representing Australia at FIFA congresses, sitting next to the small Caribbean nation of Aruba — "a population of a hundred thousand people."

"Behind us would be Brazil … millions of people, an absolute icon of world football … but everyone gets one vote; that's where your confederation structure comes into play," he said.

Mr Gallop believes the president's political future will depend on whether member associations believe the successes achieved under his leadership outweigh the damage caused by the failed privatisation proposal.

" Whether there's enough credit in the bank for all the good things that FIFA have produced … or whether this has blown them up will remain to be seen. "

Fan outrage

Patrick Clancy, head of the Football Supporters Association in Australia, told 7.30 many fans felt betrayed by the proposal.

Football's governing body has long been at the centre of controversy and corruption allegations. (REUTERS: Arnd Wiegmann )

"He's tried to privatise football at the expense of the game of football," he said.

"It's something that came out of nowhere and is not in line with what anyone has thought of before. And so I think that's the concern; where's it all going?"

His organisation is now very keen to understand where Football Australia stands on Mr Infantino and his leadership.

"These are very troubling times in world football and Football Australia needs to make its position very clear," he said.

Mr Clancy says football supporters want to see the game run properly.

"They want to feel that there is a degree of integrity and they don't want a money-hungry organisation that seems to be interfering with that organic nature of the game," he said.

"Within 24 hours, Infantino and FIFA completely changed the shape of world football.

" They blindsided almost everyone in the game, so goodness knows what's going to happen in the next seven days. "

World.title: Australia's coach says no tour match ahead of India Test series
World.content:
Australia will again opt for a training camp ahead of the five-Test tour of India rather than play ​a traditional warm-up match before attempting to end a 22-year wait for a Test series victory on the subcontinent.

Australia also chose not to play a tour match before ​the 2023 series, ‌instead training on specially prepared, spin-friendly pitches in Bengaluru before the opening Test.

The decision drew scrutiny after India won the Nagpur opener by an innings ‌and 132 runs, setting the tone for a 2-1 series ⁠victory that allowed the hosts to retain the Border-Gavaskar ‌Trophy.

Ifs, buts and maybes for Australia in India The record books will show that Australia left India without the Border-Gavaskar Trophy, but the series defeat offers plenty of opportunity for introspection ahead of the Ashes.

Head coach Andrew McDonald ​said Australia would scout ‌a location to immerse themselves in conditions similar to India before the series opener in Nagpur starting on January 21.

"We've got a couple of options there," he told Cricket Australia website Cricket.com.au ​on ‌Wednesday.

"We have gone to the UAE previously and we have also gone into India last time into Bengaluru, so we're ⁠just working through what that ‌would look like in terms ‌of how we then manage the individuals."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Australia has not won a Test ‌series in India since 2004 when Adam Gilchrist's side triumphed 2-1.

Australia have a gruelling schedule before they ‌arrive in ​India, with a ⁠two-Test home series starting against Bangladesh in Darwin next week followed by a three-Test tour of South Africa in October and another four-Test home series against New Zealand from December ⁠9.

Fast bowler Michael Neser has been ruled out of the Bengaluru series with a ‌calf strain suffered ‌at training in Brisbane but McDonald said wicketkeeper-batter ​Josh Inglis was expected to be available after recovering from a back spasm.
